JOHN F. LOWE

Grand Master
September 23, 2012 – October 6, 2013

II

JOHN F. LOWE

Grand Master – 2012-2013
John Frederick Lowe was installed as Grand Master on September 23, 2012.
John is a Past Master of Oxnard Lodge No. 341 and of Irvine Valley
Lodge No. 671 in Lake Forest. Born in Oxnard, California, he graduated from
Moorpark Community College in 1970 with a degree in Liberal Arts and he
studied business administration at California State University, Northridge.
A third-generation Mason, John was raised a Master Mason in his fathers’
lodge, Oxnard No. 341, in 1981. He served as Master there in 1989. Later, John
affiliated with Irvine Valley Lodge No. 671, where he served as Master in 2000.
John also served as an Officer’s Coach at both lodges, and in 2004 was presented
the Hiram Award from Irvine Valley Lodge. John served the lodges in his area as
a District Inspector from 1990-1993.
Since 1989, John has served on several Grand Lodge committees
including the Leadership Development Committee, for which he was chairman
from 2007 through 2009. John has been a member of the board of trustees for the
Acacia Creek Masonic senior living community, California Masonic Memorial
Temple, the Masonic Homes of California and the Nob Hill Masonic Center; he
also served as president of the California Masonic Foundation. John served as
Junior Grand Deacon for Most Worshipful M. William Holsinger in 2003 and as
Grand Orator for Most Worshipful David R. Doan in 2005.
John is a member of numerous Masonic organizations. He is a 32º
Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in the Scottish Rite Valley of Ventura.
He is a member of Al Malaikah Shriners in Los Angeles; Dr. Rob Morris Chapter
Order of the Eastern Star in Santa Monica; the Southern California Past Masters
Association; the National Sojourners, Santa Ana – El Toro Chapter; and is also a
Hero of ’76. He is a member of all three York Rite bodies in Orange County and
of the Saint Gabriel Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine. In 2011, he was
awarded the DeMolay Honorary Legion of Honor.
Supporting the Department of Defense for nearly 35 years, John
is a department manager at Northrop Grumman Corporation, where he
leads employees providing logistic support services for both manned and
unmanned aircraft.
John and Becky, his wife of 40 years, live in Aliso Viejo, California.
They have two adult sons, two daughters-in-law, and four grandchildren.

One Hundred Sixty-Fourth
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, October 4, 2013
The 164th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
John F. Lowe on Friday, October 4, 2013.
Worshipful Brother Francis A. Russell, Jr. Richard J. Modolo, Past
Master of Placerville Lodge No. 26, raised the opening session of Grand Lodge.
The gavel used to raise Grand Lodge was presented to the Grand Master at the
Installation of Officers of Placerville Lodge.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at
the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, following
which the Grand Master, accompanied by the Deputy Grand Master, personally
greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our
Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters
were then escorted to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master
then directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the
usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

Video Presentation
The Grand Lodge of California premiered a new video entitled “The
First Great Light: the Holy Scriptures and Freemasonry.” This ten-minute video
presentation explores the role of Holy Writings within Freemasonry, tracing their
history and traditions, as well as studying the deeply personal symbolism they
bring to each member of our global brotherhood. Masonic and religious scholars
from a variety of faiths will guide us through an investigation into the fascinating
relationship between Masonry and the Holy Writings.
At 4:55 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 5.

12

Proceedings of the
Memorial Service

The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Randall L. Brill, Grand
Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren.
My brothers, we pause in our doings this morning to dedicate a few
moments to those who, the past year, have been called from labor to refreshment
and have taken their places in the Celestial Lodge above. During the last twelve
months, 486 of our brothers in this Grand Lodge have entered into the eternal care
of the Almighty. They have laid down their trowels and left the quarries of life in
the unwavering confidence that the Supreme Grand Master fulfills His promise of
life everlasting to His faithful. Let those of us present take these few moments to
search our hearts and memories in order to recall those departed personally known
to us, to remember their service to our gentle Craft in general and our lodges in
particular, and the influence that their examples had on our own lives. Let us vow
this day to remember and honor them by never forgetting our obligations to those
still with us. Let us remember to show our appreciation, express our respect, and
offer our aid to the brethren we respect and admire before they are called home to
join the Creator. Let us determine to pay heed to and rightfully honor the living
now rather than waiting for them to join the dead. In so doing may we best honor
those who have gone on ahead.
Heavenly Father, we address You this morning in the firm belief that
You have welcomed our brothers into Your eternal loving care. We know
that You have made soft and safe their places of rest and will reward
them with eternal glory, happiness, and peace. Grant that in our own
passing we too will depart from this world in the comfort of faith and the
anticipation of eternal life. Amen

Most Worshipful Frank Loui, Past Grand Master, delivered a eulogy for
the late Past Grand Master, Homer Douglas Lemons.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

13

Eulogy
Homer Douglas Lemons
Most Worshipful Homer Douglas Lemons, the 115th grand master of
Masons in California and Hawaii, was born in Okmulgee, Okla. (36 miles south
of Tulsa, Okla.) on May 29, 1925. His father was an oil field driller and as new
fields were discovered, the family followed them, moving often. In his childhood,
Doug attended as many as 10 different schools in a single semester.
In 1946, Doug married Maxine Hemme, with whom he settled in Long
Beach in 1949. Doug and Maxine enjoyed a happy life in Long Beach, where
they raised two daughters, Debra and Linda, and one son, Stephen. Following in
his father’s footsteps, Doug also worked in the energy industry. He distinguished
himself in an accomplished career, retiring as manager and chief engineer of
Gammaloy, Ltd. – a subsidiary of the Cree Oil Company.
Doug enjoyed a fulfilling life in Masonry as well. He petitioned BixbyKnolls Lodge No. 699 (now Long Beach Lodge No. 327) to receive his degrees,
and was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on May 28, 1958. He
served as master with distinction to his lodge in 1966. Being the ritualist that
he was, Doug served as inspector of the 625th Masonic District from 1966 to
1969, was appointed assistant grand lecturer in August 1970, and was elected to
the office of grand lecturer that same year. His outstanding leadership qualities
were further recognized when he was elected junior grand warden in October
1977, from which station he progressed through the Grand Lodge elective offices,
culminating in his installation as grand master in October 1980.
Most Worshipful Doug was a firm advocate of changing or removing
outdated and counter-productive laws and policies. He continually sought new
inspirational methods and programs to strengthen the fraternal fiber of our craft
and to promote bonds of brotherly love and affection among our members.
Doug was the chief architect and designer of the “Layman’s Night
Program” (now known as On The Level), designed to educate non-Masons
about Freemasonry’s aims, purposes, and goals. During his year as grand master,
he established the first Masonic Leadership Council, uniting the leaders of all
Masonic bodies to work together to benefit Masonry. He also created candidate
education materials, including the “Wardens’ Workbook” and “Stated Meeting
Flip Book” for use and training of masters and wardens, as well as a Grand
Lodge information booklet to assist first-time attendees to the Grand Lodge
Annual Communication.
Doug was a firm believer and supporter of the Masonic youth orders,
frequently visiting bethels, chapters, and assemblies throughout the state. During
his tenure as grand master he would bring as many as 125 brothers with him on
these visits to demonstrate the fraternity’s support of youth activities.

14

Proceedings of the

Doug joined the Scottish Rite in Long Beach in 1967 and was honored
with the rank and decoration of inspector general honorary of the 33º degree in
1975. He was appointed deputy of the Supreme Council in California on March
13, 1987 and elected sovereign grand inspector general in California and an
active member of the Supreme Council, Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite
of Freemasonry for the Southern Masonic Jurisdiction of the United States of
America on Oct. 21, 1987, during the biennial session. He was past lieutenant
grand commander for several terms. Doug retired as an active member at the end
of 2005, and was elected an emeritus member of the Supreme Council.
On November 1, 2007, Doug’s beloved wife, Maxine, passed away.
Doug laid down his working tools on January 25, 2013. He will continue to be
deeply missed by all.
We will forever remember Doug for his energetic and heartfelt pursuit
of programs to educate and inform Masons and non-Masons alike as to what
Masonry stands for and his tireless and unselfish efforts to champion the craft. His
legacy will live on in the lives of his brethren, family, and community who were
cheered and inspired by his dedication, wisdom, and company.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

17

Most Worshipful Larry L. Adamson, Past Grand Master, delivered a
eulogy for the late Past Grand Master, Melville Howard Nahin.

Eulogy
Melville Howard Nahin
“And I think to myself, what a wonderful world” (Mel’s Theme Song).
Our world lost one of its greatest champions, and Masonry lost one of its most
dedicated servants with the passing of Most Worshipful Melville Howard Nahin
on February 18, 2013. A loving and devoted husband, father, grandfather, a
dedicated professional and a tireless laborer and leader in the quarries of our
ancient and honorable craft.
Mel was born in Chicago, Illinois on July 19, 1929 and moved to
California at an early age with his mother and older brother, the late famed
sportscaster, Stu Nahan. Mel attended Los Angeles public schools and graduated
from UCLA where he was a member of Pi Lambda Phi, the first non-sectarian
fraternity in the United States, accepting men of good character without regard to
race or religion. He was engaged in the practice of law from July, 1953 until his
recent retirement.
He met the love of his life in 1948 at a party that he and Alice both
attended with dates of their own. As Alice relates, Mel found the ideal moment
that night when his date was engaged in conversation with a group of others
and Alice’s date was away from her side to sneak over to Alice and obtain her
phone number.
Alice and Mel were married two years later in 1950 while Mel was
attending Loyola Law School. MW Mel established his law practice in 1953 and
completed 59 years of service this last year.
They were married more than 63 years and had two sons, Bruce and
Richard, as well as four grandchildren.
Mel had two very real loves in his life; his family and Freemasonry. In
Freemasonry, there was little he didn’t accomplish, and his biography is testimony
to his faith, allegiance and exemplary leadership.
He became a Mason on July 12, 1954 in Ionic Lodge No. 520 (now
Ionic–Composite), and served as its Master in 1966. The Lodge honored him
as the first recipient of the Isadore Moore Masonic Service Award in 1972, his
lodge’s Vierling Kersey Award for Outstanding Contributions to Youth in 1981
and the Hiram Award in 1995. He was also a member of Riviera Lodge No. 780,
Wisdom Lodge No. 202, and the Lodge of the HolyLands #10, Grand Lodge
of Israel.

18

Proceedings of the

Mel was a noted Masonic author contributing regularly to the Scottish
Rite Journal, the California Freemason, and the Indiana Freemason. He was a
member of the Stephen S. Wise Temple in Los Angeles.
Mel devoted much time and effort to the Order of DeMolay. He served as
the Chairman of the Executive Committee for the Southern California Jurisdiction,
as well as its legal counsel for 25 years.
Mel was Venerable Master of the Los Angeles Lodge of Perfection in
1984. He served for many years as its Chairman of the Childhood Language
Disorders Clinic. For 12 years, he was the Vice President of the California
Scottish Rite Foundation. He was coroneted in 1981 with the Thirty-Third Degree,
Honorary. He served for 12 years as a member of the Board of Governors of the
Los Angeles Shriners Hospital, serving two years as its Chairman.
Mel also had important roles in the Masonic Service Bureau, Bush
Memorial Foundation, Southern California Past Masters Association and his
Shrine Club. He was an Honorary Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Iran
in Exile.
Most Worshipful Nahin served our grand jurisdiction his entire Masonic
life. He served on or chaired 12 different committees of our Grand Lodge and
served as Grand Orator for MW Robert West in 1981. He was paid the ultimate
honor and affirmation when he was elected and installed Grand Master and served
as the 133rd Grand Master of our Grand Jurisdiction in 1998.
Mel will always be remembered for his bold and daring presentation of
Swan Lake with his G/L officers on the stage of Grand Lodge in 1999. Although
he attempted to set a precedent for those of us who followed as Grand Master,
he remains the only Grand Master to adorn a tutu and pink tights in their official
capacity as GM.
Many of us view Most Worshipful Mel’s principle legacy as Grand
Master as his introduction of our Basic Masonic Education Course which Grand
Lodge authorized with the adoption of his Recommendation No. 5. With the
shortening of the proficiencies which the candidate was required to recite back to
the lodge from memory, Mel proposed that each candidate take a written course
after each degree to deepen his knowledge of the craft and then complete an open
book examination. What is clearly a continuing tribute to Mel is the new on-line
Basic Masonic Education Course now being rolled out addressing what and how
Masons want to learn today. You’ll see Mel’s great idea is being carried forward
again for today’s Freemasonry.
Mel loved the life he was given, loved people and possessed a smile
and laugh that would brighten anyone’s day. His physical stature was certainly
not indicative of his personality and character. In those regards, he was a giant.
To know him was to love him because he knew that the value of one’s life is not
judged by material pursuits, but rather by enduring relationships and genuine care
for one another.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

19

In Most Worshipful Mel’s farewell address as our Grand Master at our
Annual Communication in 1999, he closed with a story about a terminally ill
woman and her pastor. While describing what she wanted for her funeral, she
told a somewhat bewildered pastor that she wanted to be buried with a fork in
her hand. When the pastor asked her to explain her wish, she told him that at all
the Church’s or other social dinners she attended, that after the main course was
served and dishes were being cleared, the servers would inevitably lean over to
her and say “Keep your fork.” That was her favorite part because it meant that
something better was about to come. She went on to say that she wants people to
see her in her casket with the fork in her hand so they would realize that for her
“the best is yet to come.”
Most Worshipful Nahin then ended his address to us that day saying,
“This is the wish with which I leave you. For you, for the Grand Lodge of
California, and for mankind…the best is yet to come.”
Until we meet again My Brother, until we meet again.

Election of Officers
The Grand Master then explained the balloting procedure for the election
of officers. No ballot would be necessary if the office was not contested. If more
than one nomination was received for an office, ballot cards would be distributed
for the purpose of balloting for that office.

carried that the nominations be closed, and that the Grand Secretary be instructed
to cast a unanimous ballot for Right Worshipful John L. Cooper III to serve as
Grand Master for the ensuing Grand Lodge year. Upon his acceptance, he was
declared unanimously elected.

Presentation of the Mark Twain Award
Since 2006, the Masonic Information Center, an arm of the Masonic
Service Association of North America, has presented the Mark Twain Award
for Excellence in Masonic Awareness to lodges across the country. This year,
two California lodges were recognized for their efforts to reach beyond their
lodge raising the awareness of Masonry in their communities. The Grand Master
recognized and congratulated California Lodge No. 1, San Francisco, and Granada
Hills Lodge No. 378, Granada Hills, for their accomplishment.
Special Recognition
The Masonic Homes of California has been an important part of our
fraternity for more than 100 years. During this time, the Masonic Home has
provided tremendous care and services to Masons and their families and to
children with and without a Masonic affiliation. Over the last ten years alone,
the Masonic Homes has provided more than $500 million dollars in services to
thousands of individuals. These services include healthy living and successful
aging for thousands of Masons, their wives and widows through residential
programs on our two senior living campuses and non-residential services through
our Masonic Outreach Programs. For the last three years, the Masonic Homes has
provided mental health care to children and families all over California through
the Masonic Center for Youth and Families. This integrated health service is not
provided anywhere else in the United States – it is truly groundbreaking. The
Masonic Homes of California continues to explore new ways to provide for the
best quality of life for all those that it serves. As you might have heard by now,
the Masonic Homes completed a nation-wide search for a new Executive Vice
President and has selected Brother Gary Charland to lead the Homes into the next
era of excellence.

32

Proceedings of the

The Homes is able to provide these services through the generosity of
California Masons, who for a century now have made annual gifts to the Home
and who have remembered the Masonic Homes in their wills and estate planning.
A gift to the Masonic Home is an investment in the quality of life of some of our
most vulnerable family members. It is an investment in our children, our families,
and our communities. When you consider how your charitable contributions can
make a difference, think of the Masonic Homes and know that your generosity
will make a profound difference.
The Grand Master thanked Most Worshipful David R. Doan, the
president of the board, and all of the trustees of the Masonic Homes of California
for their sponsorship of the program tonight.
Keynote Address
The Masons of California can be very proud of the Masonic Leadership
Program, developed to define what leadership means to California Masons and
to encourage all members of the fraternity to act as Masonic leaders. The new
approach was developed out of the fraternity’s strategic initiatives to improve
the members experience, strengthen management and governance effectiveness
at all levels. As a former chairman of the Grand Lodge leadership development
committee, the Grand Master has taken a special interest in our leadership
programs over the last ten years. The Grand Master is also very proud to be the
first Grand Master of California to reside in Orange County while serving as
Grand Master. When you think of Orange County, you must think of Disney. You
might also know that Disney has a world-renowned leadership program. Tonight
we are very privileged to have with us a leader in the Disney Institute who will
present “The Disney Approach to Leadership Excellence”.
Bruce Kimbrell serves as the site leader for Disney Institute West Coast
operations, headquartered in Anaheim. In this role, Bruce works with international
and domestic clients to develop specialized Disney Institute programming to fit
specific needs. Bruce’s passion for helping companies improve business practices
has taken him around the world to locations such as Chile, Dubai, England, and
many parts of the U.S.
Bruce began his Disney career as a skipper on the world-famous Jungle
Cruise at the Disneyland Resort in Anaheim before embarking on the Disneyland
Management Training Program. It was that decision that set him up for a dynamic
leadership career at The Walt Disney Company. Bruce served Disneyland in a
variety of leadership roles.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

33

Bruce is the author of “Walt Disney and You,” an internal training
program designed to re-connect current Disney cast members with the ideals and
founding principles of Walt Disney. The primary video used in this presentation
won the U.S. Corporate Recognition Award for the Walt Disney Company in 2004
and has been presented world-wide.
A graduate of Brigham Young University, Bruce earned a degree in
public relations and communication.

“Beyond the Lodge” Grand Lodge 2013
On behalf of the Job’s Daughters of California I would like to thank you,
Most Worshipful Grand Master John Lowe, Grand Lodge Officers, and Members
of our wonderful Masonic Family for all of your support, and making it possible
for young women to have a place where they can learn leadership skills, public
speaking, self-confidence, charitable service, and respect for elders. Because of
your hard work in going “Beyond the Lodge” this year, by gaining more members,
more young girls can have the opportunity to enjoy what I would call my home
away from home…Job’s Daughters.
I joined Job’s Daughters five years ago because of an elderly man who
wore a ring, but it was not his wedding band, it was his Masonic ring. He wore
it with honor, pride, and respect everyday, and because of that simple ring, I am
standing in front of you today. How you ask? My father took note of it, and asked
what kind of ring it was. Because of that simple ring it grew to a simple question.
Now my father is a Mason, my sister and I are Past Honored Queen’s of Bethel
No. 24 San Pedro, and were previous Sweethearts for our DeMolay Chapter. Also
my Mother, Father and I are members of our local Eastern Star Chapter. This is
what I like to call the beginning of my three-step plan “the Circle of Masonic
Family Life.”
Because of my motto “We are all on a journey to find our Inner Swan”
Step one is Hatch an egg of an idea:
•

Telling neighbors and family friends about the Masonic Orders is like
hatching an egg. It might help them to see what the Masonic Family can

Proceedings of the
offer them as a whole. We have something that many groups do not have,
because there are different orders for different ages. Why I think we have
a growing problem is because we just want that child or that adult, but
our goal should be working together to welcome that family into our
Masonic orders.

Step 2: Support, and lead.
•

This new family, much like a cygnet needs to be led by a swan. We,
as members need to show them, lead them, and support them. But do
not forget about supporting your local Job’s Daughters, Rainbows Girls,
and DeMolay by attending their meetings, Installations, and receptions

Step 3: The Full Circle
•

Now these young women, and men have out grown their youth
organizations. So you need to remind them of the adult Masonic Orders,
and welcome them so that they will continue with their faithful journey,
and eventually become the leaders to new incoming members. Also by
keeping them faithful, their children become of age and restart the circle
of Masonic Life. Remember we do not just want that daughter, son or
adult, but to go “Beyond the Lodge” and work together to welcome that
family into our Masonic family.

If we all work together to support each other, I believe that membership
in all of our orders will begin to flourish.

On behalf of all the young men of Northern California DeMolay, I would

NorCal’s theme for this year has been “Doctor Who: Doing Good for
Humanity and for DeMolay” and we as DeMolays have strived to improve our
Chapters, our communities, and others around us, just like the good Doctor does
in his travels across time and space.
Our themes hold close similarities. We have been going “Beyond the
Chapter”, just as you have in your Lodges, with numerous efforts with our
philanthropic project this year, The California Association of Food Banks. Many
of our Chapters, like San Francisco with San Francisco Lodge #120, have gone
out to their local Food Bank to assist in any way they can, to help those less
fortunate to have a full stomach when they are down on their luck. The Masons
of California have done many good deeds to help inspire the minds of children
when you donate books to classrooms, so that kids who may not be so lucky

your efforts.
Will all Senior DeMolays please raise their hands? *pause* Okay, who
knows how many Master Masons there are in California? The CA Masons website
proudly states that there are over 60,000. Who can guess how many DeMolays are
in the state? Is it half or maybe a fourth of how many Masons there are? I wish.
Maybe an eighth? That’s about 7,500 and you would still be wrong. It’s not 1/16
but, rounding up, it is close to 1 DeMolay for every 32 Master Masons. There
are young men in many cities that go without the chance to become a DeMolay
simply because there is no Chapter there for them. How many great young men
go through life without the opportunity to be a part of the Masonic Family? Could
it be more than 60,000 Masons if there were more young men, who through their
involvement in DeMolay, petitioned to join lodge, like the many men that raised
their hands? If DeMolay and the Masonic Family are not there to help guide a
young teen, what will he become when he reaches the manhood years of life?
I know that the Masons of California have been one of the best supporters of
DeMolay in all of the United States and of many children and inspiring them to
read more, but WE need your help now more than ever. I ask you to go beyond the
lodge and be in a young man’s life, support your local DeMolay Chapter or help
sponsor one if there is not one in your area.

“Beyond the Lodge”
Most Worshipful John F. Lowe, honored guests, family, friends, and my
brethren of the craft.
Thank you for allowing me to speak at this year’s Grand Lodge. Our
theme this year for Southern California DeMolay is Lord of the Rings: Fellowship
of the Crown. This theme was chosen for two main reasons. The first being that
in the first degree of DeMolay each boy symbolically wears the same Crown
of Youth, dedicated to the seven cardinal virtues of the order; love of parents,
reverence for sacred things, courtesy, comradeship, fidelity, cleanness, and
patriotism. Each boy symbolically wearing this crown shows that no matter who
we are, or where we come from, we are all equal in the eyes of DeMolay, just as
we are all created equal by the Supreme Architect of the Universe.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

39

The second reason is that in the fourth section of our second degree it
is said that we are a fellowship, for service, which we are, a band of brothers,
dedicated not only to improving ourselves but to improving the world as well. We
truly are a fellowship of the crown.
This year’s Grand Lodge theme, “Beyond the Lodge,” has so much
meaning to the members of the Order of DeMolay, for it was because of a Mason
who went beyond his lodge that our order was formed. The founder of our order,
Frank Sherman Land, was an active member of Ivanhoe Lodge number 446
in the state of Kansas. He saw that the young men of his community needed
a fatherly figure to look up to, for their fathers had gone off to fight in World
War One, many of whom would make the supreme sacrifice, leaving behind their
beloved families.
Being the exemplary Mason he was, Frank Land went beyond the lodge
to help the young men of his community, and eventually the world, by creating a
group dedicated to serving young men and giving them fatherly figures they could
emulate and strive to be like. Brother Land eventually became known as “Dad”
to many people around the US and the title “DAD” quickly became associated
with DeMolay.
In life, no matter the rank or distinction which a man may achieve, his
most important title will forever be “Dad.” To be called a dad by the young men
of DeMolay is an honor, for it shows that you are a role model and looked at as a
father figure by the young men of the future. As a “Dad” you are a representative
of what Dad Land was to the young men of his time.
I am proud to call each of you “DAD” whether you are an advisor of
DeMolay or not, for you are a Mason, a man who is looked up to, a man who is
respected and revered by the young men of DeMolay. Dad Land went beyond the
lodge to assist the young men of his community. Dad Land went beyond the lodge
to be a “DAD” to the young men of the world. Dad Land went beyond the lodge
to create an order that has changed the lives of millions of young men. Dad Land
went beyond the lodge, not because he had to, but because he saw that he was
needed. Dad Land went beyond the lodge, and he will be forever remembered by
DeMolays and Masons alike as one of the most respectable men in history, not
because of his many personal accolades and honors, but because he set out to help
the young men who he knew would be not only the future of the world, but also
the future of Freemasonry.
This one man changed the world in 1919 by going beyond the lodge.
Now, imagine what you can do for our youth by going beyond the lodge.
Thank you.
The Grand Master thanked Michael for his remarks and presented a
donation on behalf of the California Masonic Foundation to be used for the benefit
of the members of Southern California DeMolay.

John L. Channon
Worshipful Brother John L. Channon, past master of Evergreen Lodge
No. 259 in Riverside and inspector of the 822nd Masonic district, has served Job’s
Daughters since becoming a master mason in 1998 at both the local and state level.
Currently, he is the Guardian Treasurer of Bethel No. 264 in Riverside. In 2012
he completed a three year term on the Finance Committee of the Grand Guardian
Council of California serving as chairman his last year on the committee.
Brother Channon’s contributions to Job’s Daughters have been many
and varied. John began his involvement with Bethel No. 264 as promoter of
sociability and then was selected as the associate bethel guardian serving from
1999 to 2011. He has been part of the Grand Bethel photography team and has
lent his professional expertise as part of the audio/visual team for many years.
John has been a ritual judge at Inland Empire and Grand Bethel competitions. His
leadership was recognized in 2009 when he was selected Grand Junior Custodian
and again in 2010 when he a was asked to serve a three year term on the Grand
Guardian Council’s Finance Committee, the last year as chairman. He is a mentor
and guide to the young women of Job’s Daughters and an advisor and leader for the
adults who serve with him as adult volunteer leaders. Brother Channon is always
there to help and work beside the dedicated members and council members. He is
a role model worthy of emulation.
Brother Channon remains an active and dedicated Masonic leader. In
addition to his duties as an inspector, he serves as the secretary and treasurer of the
Division 8 Raising A Reader fundraising committee and the Inland Empire Public
Schools Advisory Committee. Brother John was recognized for his service to his
lodge and Freemasonry with the Hiram Award in 2006.
Jairo J. Gomez
Worshipful Brother Jairo J.Gomez, is a past master of Morning Star
Lodge No. 19 in Stockton and inspector of the 428th Masonic district. He is
also the chairman of the advisory council for Stockton Chapter, Northern
California DeMolay.

Brother Gomez was raised a master mason in 2005. He quickly and
enthusiastically became a vital member of the Masonic family. While advancing
through the chairs of his lodge to become master, he has served as worthy
patron of Stockton Oaks Chapter No. 50 of the Order of Eastern Star, became a
member of the York Rite Bodies and Scottish Rite Bodies serving as the Assistant
Personal Representative of the Sovereign Grand Inspector General for the Valley
of Stockton. Because of his mentoring, leadership, and never give up attitude,
Brother Jairo has transformed Stockton Chapter from a struggling chapter to an

Glenn Martin
Worshipful Brother Glenn Martin, is a past master of Yorba Linda Lodge
No. 469 and is the “Trailer and Technical Assistant” to the Supreme Inspector
for the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls in California, Mrs. Sara
Lee Martin.
Brother Martin is an exemplar of service and love. For over thirty
years he has been an active supporter of the Rainbow Girls in Orange County
and throughout the state of California. Currently, Glenn is in his third year on
the advisory board for Fullerton-Yorba Linda Assembly. Previously, he has been
chairperson of the advisory board and has been Rainbow Dad on numerous

countless meetings, retreats, swim parties, work parties, and social events. It is the

Inspector, he traverses the state and the country serving as taxi driver, file clerk,

advisor. He can rightly be called “the wind beneath the wings” of California’s
Rainbow Girls and their adult advisors and supporters.
Brother Martin is a role model for Masons everywhere. His commitment
to the Masonic youth orders extends beyond his service to the International Order
of the Rainbow for Girls. In 2009, he was recognized with a DeMolay Honorary
Legion of Honor. He actively seeks to help the youth orders work together to
achieve their mission and vision of Masonic youth being tomorrow’s leaders.

Donald E. Travis
Brother Donald E. Travis, is a fifty year member of Montebello-Whittier
Lodge No. 323, serving twenty-five years as treasurer. In 1997, he was recognized
with the Hiram Award for his many years of service to the lodge and to the
Masonic family.
Brother Travis began his Masonic experience as a young man when he
joined Montebello Chapter, Order of DeMolay. As a youth leader, he served as
master councilor of his chapter. An outstanding ritualist, he presided as installing
officer for numerous installations, performed the Flower Talk regularly, and took
part in the Majority Service for those DeMolays reaching age 21. As an adult
leader, Brother Travis worked with chapters for many years as an advisor and
has been recognized by DeMolay for his outstanding efforts as a youth and adult
with the Degree of Chevalier, the Cross of Honor, and the DeMolay Legion of
Honor. Brother Don’s primary focus has been the development and continuance
of the Crossroads DeMolay Court of Chevaliers where he was first grand
commander and then secretary/treasurer for forty years. He has been the glue
that has kept this court together organizing the annual observances, maintaining
membership records, being the point of contact for other chevaliers, and forming
investiture teams.
For more than forty years, it has been Brother Travis’ mission and goal
to continue the camaraderie and fraternal bond of DeMolay that he experienced as
a young man and to see that an important institution of the Order of DeMolay be
sustained to recognize the leadership and service of active and senior DeMolays
in Southern California.

Grand Master’s Message
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California:
Past Grand Masters, Past Grand Officers, Grand Officers, Worshipful
Masters, my brethren all.
Welcome to the 164th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
California, here in the City and County of San Francisco.
When I stood before you following installation September last, I
promised that as your Grand Master I would be leading from the middle. I am
here to deliver on that promise: leading from the middle!
Here we are, the living, breathing embodiment of modern Freemasonry.
When I look out upon you, I see brothers, friends, family. I see the traces of
centuries of men before us, who were devoted to this fraternity and trusted that
someday, in centuries to come, it would still resemble the one they built. If they
are looking down upon us today, I am sure they feel proud.
I extend a warm fraternal welcome to those who have traveled from
other jurisdictions to be with us this weekend. You exemplify Masonry’s global
network, in action. I am humbled by your attendance. We are indeed grateful that
you’re here, and we hope you enjoy San Francisco.
It is an honor to address you today and share the condition of our craft
with you, one of my final responsibilities as your grand master. My theme as grand
master was Beyond the Lodge -- and, fittingly, that is where this year took me.
After all of the travels and events, degrees and installations, 50-year pins, youth
order meetings, cornerstone ceremonies and dedications, and visits to Masonic
jurisdictions from Oregon to Missouri, I am eager to share my impressions of
California Masonry in the year 2013.
But first, to explain what I learned this year, I must begin with history.
We know that during the 1940s, we became experts at taking new
members from application through Master Mason degree in short time spans. Of
course this was an expedient, due to the exigencies of wartime. Members both old
and new were shipping off to foreign shores.
In the 1950s into the early 1960s, men still joined as we moved to the
apex of our membership numbers… And then times, they began a-changing.
When the baby-boomer generation came of age, thoughts of joining the
fraternity were overshadowed by trips to foreign places such as Viet Nam. As was
said then, we didn’t trust anyone over 30. Then move forward to the 1970s and

50

Proceedings of the

1980s... our new member rates continually got smaller. And yet we still measured
ourselves again by how fast we moved men from application to Master Mason,
even though there was no external pressure for speed as in earlier decades.
Nonetheless, it seems speed was all we knew. Yes, we even gave awards
for conferring the most degrees in a year.
Then, the new millennium dawned, and young men of a new generation
began petitioning for the degrees; but with a crucial difference. These young men,
in their 20s and 30s, do not feel the “need for speed.”
They want to enjoy being an Entered Apprentice for a time, with patience.
To understand the meanings of our teachings for that degree. Then when it feels
right, to ask lodge leadership for their Fellow Craft degree. And then, the same
effect: Be a Fellow Craft and study the meaning of that degree before moving to
Master Mason.
Understanding – understanding the essence of Freemasonry, not calendar
days – is the measurement on their mind.
So what does this mean? Certainly with stated meetings now held in the
first degree, there is no need to rush to Master Mason in order to attend business
meetings. Grand Lodge is no longer pressuring for speed, but rather cultivating
quality, engagement, and lifelong learning. Awards drive behavior; let us not
count total degrees, let’s count engaged members. Engaged for a lifetime.
I submit that today a sign of good lodge health is a backlog of Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts that are not yet scheduled for their next degree.
Yes, a backlog. It’s okay to have a backlog. Now this new reality does require
lodge leadership to ensure that these fellows are engaged in lodge activities. To
ensure that they are engaged in learning the lessons we provide before moving to
the next level. That they are not being merely coached, but being mentored and
helped by a friend and brother. And then, only then, when the time is right, to
confer upon them a quality degree that builds even more engagement and learning.
My brothers, this is the new reality. This is brotherhood in the 21st century. This is
leadership found in the greatest jurisdiction across Freemasonry.
For the purposes of this report, I will also share the following: California
lodges conferred more than 3,700 degrees in total this year, and we gained more
than 2,000 new members. While our total losses were nearly double that number,
let us look at loss due to death: during our fiscal year we lost 2,051 brothers – many
of that greatest generation. Our total gain was 2,424, so in the pure measurement
of new income versus death, we have indeed turned the corner. Soon we will be
stable, and then growing once again
The two lodges that received their charters at last year’s Annual
Communication were constituted: Oasis Lodge No. 854 and Veritas Lodge No.
855. Oasis meets in downtown Los Angeles; brethren who work in that area now

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

51

have a lodge home within a convenient distance. Veritas has taken residence in
San Juan Capistrano, a city that never has had a Masonic presence. Now Veritas is
filling that need in South Orange County. Destiny Lodge UD, which meets at the
Covina Masonic Home, was instituted on August 30. Sadly, seven charters were
arrested, and happily two were restored.
Of course, numbers can only quantify. The California Masons that I met
this year showed me the bigger picture. In California, our lodges are made up with
the highest caliber of men. We are working hard to keep it that way. We changed
the candidate application process this year in a few important ways. One, we
introduced new applications for degrees and affiliation, designed to improve the
prospect and applicant experience. We also transformed the character investigation
process. We introduced new character investigations, and developed training
resources and a video to support and instruct investigators. We are learning more
about candidates from the start, and giving them an opportunity to learn more
about us. As a result, the men who take their first degree are more prepared to
embark on their Masonic journey.
This work is but one part of our strategic plan. In this fourth year of the
five-year plan, we made a number of major advances. I’ll share a couple of the
most significant.
We developed an online candidate education program, an interactive
learning system that will transform Masonic education for candidates. Now, when
a candidate wants to learn about a Masonic symbol, he will see a picture of it. He
will read a paper about it. He will take a quiz to test his knowledge of its use in
the ritual. He will be guided to more articles, videos, and resources about it. Our
fraternity’s brightest minds contributed thousands of hours to create this program.
We are proud to announce that, as of this weekend, online candidate education is
ready to debut. Test it out for yourself tomorrow: From 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. tomorrow,
go to the online candidate education booth, located on the far wall of the Exhibit
Hall. You’ll also receive an email announcement with all the details shortly after
this weekend.
The California Masonic Symposium, held in two locations, educated
more than 300 brothers and friends of the fraternity on an important crossroads
in our history: the rise and fall of the Antient and Modern grand lodges. We cohosted another international conference at UCLA, bringing Masonic scholars
from across the globe together to share research and ideas.
Lodge treasurers and secretaries will know that earlier this year, Grand
Lodge rolled out Intacct, a new accounting and reporting solution for California
lodges and hall associations.
California Masons have repeatedly stepped forward in support of
public schools, championing programs so that every child might have an equal
opportunity to pursue knowledge. We continue to build on this legacy today.

52

Proceedings of the

This year, we gave $773,000 in Investment in Success scholarships to some very
deserving California students: high school seniors who have succeeded at school
despite immense financial and social challenges. Many are the first in their family
to go to college. The Investment in Success scholarship is special; it not just about
providing the financial means for college access. Rather, our goal for these students
is college success. This success will lead to their being strong, contributing adults
to the future of our great state. Our goal remains to connect every scholarship
student with all available resources, including college counseling and academic
support services. Their success is our success.
One of your strategic plan mandates is the desire for a statewide program
for public school support. This is so important that it cannot be a grand master’s
project; it must be your project, the fraternity’s project. And, as I traveled
throughout the state, you embraced this change to make it personal to you and
your lodge. And so, our partnership with Raising A Reader is the program you
have taken as your own. Engaged parents are the heart of education. They close
achievement gaps. They level the playing field for academic success. By embracing
this knowledge and using reading as a bonding tool for families, Raising A Reader
has become one of the most successful literacy and family engagement programs
in the country. By the end of this school year, we will have brought the program
to nearly 7,000 elementary-school children and their families. That’s 7,000
California families who will be more engaged in their child’s education. That’s
7,000 California children with the early literacy tools and family support that they
need to succeed in school, and thrive in the future. My brothers, you are creating
a brighter future for these children and families. You are moving the needle of
literacy to the right side. You are instilling a culture of literacy in California. This
year alone, 103 lodges contributed more than $281,000 to the partnership.
And what about the Bay Area Masons? They decided five years ago
to make a difference in children’s sports programs; that partnership is with the
Junior Giants Foundation. Children up and down the state are benefitted by this
foundation’s programs to teach sportsmanship, citizenship, and teamwork. Our
guys decided that every child in the program should have a baseball glove. Last
month at AT&T Park here in San Francisco, we presented a check for $83,000
to the foundation, enough to buy more than 4,000 gloves. Over the past five
years, Masons for Mitts has provided $274,000, making us the largest fundraiser
donating to the Junior Giants. My brothers, you are making a difference, one
glove at a time.
Last year, our attendance at leadership retreats soared nearly 20
percent from the previous year. In 2013, we held steady near that record, with
606 Masons and spouses and partners attending retreats, and another 600-plus
Masons attending at least one of our Lodge Management Certification Programs.
Almost two out of every three lodges participated in the Secretary & Treasurer or
Master & Wardens Retreats. That’s a good rate, and we will continue to make it
even better.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

53

If you were among those who attended a retreat, you know that we
also launched the Masonic Leadership Project this year to rejuvenate leadership
throughout the fraternity. Each of us is called to be a leader in our life, whether
in our family, our work, our community, or our lodge. Masons take this charge
seriously. So we decided to develop training to lead as a Mason. The project began
with a survey to 30,000 California brothers. During each retreat, you also shared
your thoughts and experiences about Masonic values and their contribution to
leadership. Through the survey and in person, you painted a picture of leadership
that is a team effort, not a race to the officer line. You told us that you care about
values and relationships. We created an all-new leadership training, with three
different courses, based on that approach. Every officer who attended a 2013
retreat received the training, and now lodges throughout California can bring the
program right to their lodge.
Masonic scholar Margaret Jacob, one of our partners at UCLA, describes
18th-century lodges on the European continent as “schools of government,”
places where early democratic habits were formed. Today, our lodges are truly
“schools of leadership.” Think of the great leaders throughout history who were
Masons. Today, the world needs those leaders more than ever, in all capacities,
on an individual and global scale. It needs men who are prepared to lead with
strength and humility, integrity and collaboration. The world needs Masons, and
it needs us to be leaders. The Masonic Leadership Project is one way that we are
answering that need.
Clearly, the crown jewels of our fraternity are our homes for our senior
brethren, their wives, and widows. Our two campuses, located in Union City and
Covina, are warm, caring, and beautiful places in which to live. Most importantly,
we must have a talented, strong, and visionary executive vice president to lead the
well-being of those seniors entrusted to our care. Following a thorough search, I
am pleased to announce that our Masonic Homes Board of Trustees has selected
Worshipful Brother Gary Charland, our Grand Standard Bearer, to take charge
and move out. Worshipful Gary brings strong experience in the healthcare field,
and we know he will lead with Masonic principles and values at the forefront.
This year, I issued a challenge to every one of you, and to myself: to go
beyond the lodge – to serve our communities. To support public schools. To make
a profound difference in California. Through the Masonic Leadership Project,
through the Raising A Reader partnership, through Masons for Mitts, through the
work that you do in your communities every day, you rose to that challenge. It’s
easy to feel pride in Masonry because of who we are – our history, our rituals,
our legacy. But this year, every day, you made me proud to be a Mason because
of what we do.
This was an inspiring and productive year for our fraternity, and a truly
unforgettable one for me. I owe an enormous debt of thanks to my executive
committee for their time, talent, and vision. I am grateful for the service of our

54

Proceedings of the

grand lodge office staff that works each day serving our lodges and brethren
withersoever dispersed. To every board president and member; and to every
committee chair and member: thank you. To our Assistant Grand Lecturers and
Inspectors overseeing our lodges: thank you. These brothers work tirelessly
behind the scenes to ensure that our ancient fraternity does not falter in these
modern times. Finally, we all know that fraternity is about family. I must thank my
Grand Family, whose support carried me through this year; whose company made
it one of the most special years of my life; and whose friendliness was shared with
every lodge we visited.
Brethren, I love this fraternity, and I have loved being your grand master.
Thank you for this honor.
Now, as we prepare for a new year and a new chapter in California
Masonry, let us summon our steadfastness and perseverance once more. As
leaders and as brothers, let us go forth and spread the light of Masonry.

Respectfully submitted,
John F. Lowe, Grand Master

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2013/2014 Grand Lodge Budget
John L. Cooper III, Deputy Grand Master

As your Deputy Grand Master, it is my duty to prepare and present to
you a budget for the upcoming fiscal year. First, let me say that I am grateful for
the support of the brethren who adopted the per capita proposal I submitted at the
2012 Annual Communication.
Since that time, I have refined the budget while monitoring current
income and expenses as well as our membership activity. Earlier this year, I
discussed the budget further with the Masters and Wardens at our retreats. Their
input over the last two years has been very helpful. I have also worked with the
Grand Lodge Finance Committee, our Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and our
finance staff to be sure that we are operating in an efficient and responsible way.
As a result of this teamwork, I now place the attached budget before you for
consideration at the upcoming Annual Communication.
At the last Annual Communication, the delegates adopted Resolution
11-07, which requires Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons to pay dues
and to be included on the rolls. Per Capita is now based on the total number of
Masons on the rolls, not just Master Masons. While our membership projections
have been very accurate over the last decade, it was very difficult to project just
how many Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons would actually be on the
rolls on June 30. As it turns out, more of these Masons remained on the rolls than
we anticipated.
Revenue for the next fiscal year is estimated to be $2,805,374. The
income includes:
•

Per Capita revenue of $1,928,736 representing 68% of the total income.

•

The dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center, which will be
approximately $210,000 or 7.5% of the total income.

•

The grant from the California Masonic Foundation in the amount of
$205,000 for Masonic education and leadership training, representing
7% of the total income.

•

The distribution from investments is $168,285, representing 6% of
total income.

•

Revenue from application fees from all lodges and dues from the Grand
Master’s Lodge totaling approximately $65,000 or two (2) percent of the
total income.

•

Other revenue from reimbursements from investments and Masonic
Service Bureaus.

70

Proceedings of the

Expenses for the next fiscal year are estimated to be $2,766,954.
These expenses are divided between fraternal, appropriations and general and
administrative. In many areas, we have kept expenses at the same level as the
current year. The following represent the changes in expenses.
•

Lodge insurance will increase by 4.8%.

•

Wages will increase by 3.0%.

•

Other employment related expenses, particularly health insurance
premiums will be up 9.8%.

•

Items subject to inflation are planned to increase by 2%-3%.

The projected net revenue after expenses is approximately $40,000.
Most of this surplus is due to the fact that we had more Masons on the rolls on
June 30 than we anticipated. Fewer Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons
demitted from our lodges than we projected.
It is unknown at this point, how many Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft Masons will be suspended for non-payment of dues in the next year. Because
of this uncertainty, I propose that we reserve $34,478 of the expected surplus to be
used in Fiscal Year 2015. This reserve will lessen the need to collect additional per
capita next year. You will notice that I have included this amount as a Fraternal
expense. As a result, the net surplus at the end of Fiscal Year 2014 should be
approximately $3,945. The California Masonic Code requires a vote of Grand
Lodge to reserve these funds for a subsequent year.
There has been a lot of thought and consideration given to this budget.
I sincerely appreciate the contributions by many different brethren. With the
adoption of this budget, we will be able to maintain the programs and services
we now provide to our lodges and members and we will make an important
investment in the future.
I thank you, again, for your previous support and ask for your support

MASONS OF CALIFORNIA
Fiscal Year 2013/2014
John L. Cooper III, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue source has been per-capita and
degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates investment income. To better
manage those monies, a four and a half-percent spending policy has been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year
valuation to ensure the preservation of the fund principle. The Grand Lodge may have other income like interest on
bank accounts and other financial instruments from time to time. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included
in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant for those
purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to
Grand Lodge by all applicants for degrees and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge manages different service
bureaus throughout the state and receives reimbursement for those expenses. The Grand Lodge also manages the
investments of its related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of those services. The Grand Lodge is
the sole shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of the corporation.

Installation Address

John L. Cooper III
Grand Master of Masons in California, 2013-2014
We are just concluding the 164th Annual Communication of our Grand
Lodge. The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
was founded in April, 1850, and while we are not the oldest Masonic Grand Lodge
in the world, 164 years is a respectable heritage. In the year 2017, just three years
from now, we will celebrate the 300th anniversary of the United Grand Lodge of
England, founded in 1717 in London. But even 300 years is not all of our history.
Our roots are lost in the mists of time, springing, according to many Masonic
historians, from stonemasons guilds of the Middle Ages in Scotland. It is certain
that our oldest written records come from Scotland, and so a 500 year history, or
more, is not beyond the realm of possibility.
So what is the meaning of an institution that well may be 500 years old,
or older. We are certainly not the same organization that we were in the mists
of antiquity, and yet we are. Our ancestors set about transforming the tools and
implements of operative Masonry into the symbols that Freemasons use today to
teach moral and ethical lessons. Masons “act upon the square” when they place
honesty and trustworthiness at the heart of their daily lives and actions; they use
the symbol of the compass to “circumscribe their desires and keep their passions
within due bounds” toward others. From that symbol comes our firm commitment
to tolerance and acceptance of the diversity of religious and political beliefs
which is a salient feature of Freemasonry. We place at the center of our meetings
a Volume of the Sacred Law as a reminder that there is a Power greater than we,
and to whom we owe our allegiance and gratitude. We use the plumb – a tool used
by our stonemason ancestors to build a wall true and straight, to remind us that
justice is an indispensable characteristic of all right-thinking men and women.
And we use the level to remind us not only that all men and women are equal in
the sight of God, but that we are traveling on the level of time to that undiscovered
country, from whose bourne no traveler returns.
Freemasonry has been described by some as a “System of morality,
veiled in allegory and illustrated by symbol.” It is that – but it is more, much
more. It becomes for us the universal moral compass that infuses our lives with
purpose and meaning. It is a journey, and the principles of Freemasonry point us
to the path that we must follow.
Such a journey is not an easy one for a Freemason. It has been welldescribed as a “rough and rugged road.” There is no easy path to virtue, and
Freemasonry requires constant practice if it is to make a difference in our lives.
Above all, Freemasonry demands perseverance – perseverance in shaping our
lives from the rough ashlar to the perfect ashlar – a stone fit for the Builder’s use
– the Great Architect’s use – in the temple of humanity.

80

Proceedings of the

I would leave you today with a poem “Anyway” which, we are told,
Mother Teresa, the apostle to the poorest of the poor, placed on her wall:
People are often unreasonable, illogical, and self-centered;
Forgive them anyway.
If you are kind, people may accuse you of selfish, ulterior motives;
Be kind anyway.
If you are successful, you will win some false friends and some true enemies;
Succeed anyway.
If you are honest and frank, people may cheat you;
Be honest and frank anyway.
What you spend years building, someone could destroy overnight;
Build anyway.
If you find serenity and happiness, they may be jealous;
Be happy anyway.
The good you do today, people will often forget tomorrow;
Do good anyway.
Give the world the best you have, and it may never be enough;
Give the world the best you’ve got anyway.
You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and your God;
It was never between you and them anyway.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2014-2015
Russell E. Charvonia, Senior Grand Warden

Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
As your Senior Grand Warden, I am responsible for preparing and
presenting to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita assessment that will
be collected in 2014 to fund the operations of Grand Lodge fiscal year for the
period of November 1, 2014 through October 31, 2015.
Beginning with my term as Junior Grand Warden, I have worked very
closely with the Executive Committee, the Finance Committee and the Grand
Lodge staff to develop projections of the income and the necessary expenses for
the 2014/2015 fiscal year. Earlier this year, I was able to share our plans with the
Masters and Wardens who attended our spring leadership retreats. I very much
appreciate the comments and input I received during and following the retreats.
At the 2012 Annual Communication Grand Lodge approved Resolution
No. 11-07, which required Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons to
pay Lodge dues. At the same time, Section 407.020 of the California Masonic
Code was amended to require that each Lodge pay per capita based on each
Mason (as opposed to each Master Mason) carried on the rolls as of June 30th
(except those whose dues had been remitted by the Lodge). As a result of this
Legislation, 10,234 Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons were added to
our membership. While nearly all of these members remained on the rolls for
2013, we are estimating that nearly 70% of them will be dropped from the active
rolls during 2014, mostly through suspensions for nonpayment of dues.
In preparing a draft budget for the 2014/2015 fiscal year, I have considered
the factors that will increase per capita, as well as those that will mitigate any
necessary increase.
The factors that will increase the per capita are:
•

•
•
•

Membership decline. We project a total loss of 7,641 billable members
(of which 6,914, or some 90%, relate to Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft Masons). This represents a loss in revenue of $244,512, or $4.65
in additional Per Capita.
Insurance. Premiums for our lodge insurance coverage will increase
by 5.7%.
Labor costs. Wages are held to a 3% increase. Health care premiums will
increase costs by an additional 5.3%.
Inflation. Items subject to inflation are expected to increase by 2% to 3%.

84

Proceedings of the
The factors that will help offset the per capita increase are the following:
•

•

Fiscal Year 2014 Per Capita Reserve. As noted in the FY 2014 budget
by the Deputy Grand Master, a Per Capita Reserve was established in
an amount of $34,478. This was made possible because the billable Per
Capita in his year was greater than previously anticipated.
Cost savings. We have identified a number of expenses that can be held
at or near last year’s levels. You will notice that the expenses in many
categories are nearly the same as the budget presented by the Deputy
Grand Master.

Thanks to the hard work and dedication of our staff, we will continue to
receive a healthy dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center from the operation
of the parking garage. And the California Masonic Foundation continues to
support our Masonic education and leadership training programs.
These factors allow us to present a balanced budget, with a per capita
assessment of $36.50. Although this represents an increase of $4.50 over the
2013/2014 assessment, it represents a lower total amount collected than the
previous year.
I very much appreciate your feedback on matters that are important to
our Craft and I thank you for your support of this Per Capita proposal.

Revenue Assumptions
PER CAPITA
There are several factors that affect Per Capita; membership levels, insurance, labor costs,
professional fees and inflation are the primary factors. The membership analysis for the
2014/2015 fiscal year projects a total loss in membership of 7,641 members. The
membership decline will result in lost revenue of $244,512 or $4.65 in additional Per Capita.
Insurance, modest labor increases along with inflation of approximately 2% to 3% accounts for
the additional Per Capita. All other things being equal, the Per Capita would have to be
increased by $4.97 to cover the effect of all of the factors discussed here. The use of the
FY14 Per Capita reserve of $34,478 will result in a $0.57 Per Capita reduction. These factors
allow us to present a balanced budget with a Per Capita of $36.50.

Report of the Grand Treasurer
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The overall financial condition of your Grand Lodge continues to be
very good due to the hard work and diligent efforts of Grand Lodge officers,
boards and committee members and the efficient Grand Lodge staff.
With a slowly strengthening economy, Grand Lodge budgets continue
to be closely monitored amid continuing efforts to conserve and curtail spending.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee continues their customary
diligence over the Grand Lodge’s investment portfolio. As a result of their
consideration of the current economic environment, they have made some wellstudied changes in the make-up and allocation of the portfolio in anticipation of
continued volatility in the economy and markets. They continue to recommend
that no more than 4.5% of the principal be distributed to the Grand Lodge
operating budget and to the other entities participating in the investment pool.
This will preserve capital in the face of future potential inflation.
Your Grand Lodge Insurance Committee applies their considerable
expertise to the ongoing risk management of the Grand Lodge and our various
entities to keep them well-protected at favorable and competitive premium costs.
The Grand Lodge Finance Committee provides advice in the development
of the Grand Lodge operating budgets and the per capita as well as advice to our
lodges. The Audit Committee determines who will audit our books and records
and provides tax services for the Grand Lodge and its related entities. The Audit
Committee also reviews the annual audits and 990 tax returns and provides an
independent report to the boards of each entity. Both committees perform their
respective duties with business-like efficiency of which any organization would
be proud.
During the past year, under the leadership of our Grand Secretary, Allan
Casalou, and Brad Colby, Director of Administration and Board Governance, all
of the boards of our Masonic entities adopted new governance policies. Since
then, each board has implemented rigorous monitoring and reporting, which
provides for greater accountability of the executive vice president to the board
through clearly defined outcomes and measurable data on results.
During the past two years, I was privileged to serve as a member of the
task force originally appointed by Most Worshipful William J. Bray III which was
charged with the duty to study Life Membership Funds. The committee, chaired
by Past Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Glenn Woody, has worked diligently to
develop legislation that will clarify and strengthen our Life Membership Program.
I urge you to give serious consideration to these resolutions.

90

Proceedings of the

Last year, legislation was passed that allowed lodges to transfer their Life
Membership Fund to the Grand Lodge for investment. As of the end of August,
five lodges have paperwork in process to transfer their funds to the Grand Lodge.
The dedicated and efficient financial staff in the Grand Lodge office
continues to provide unexcelled service in the management and reporting on the
financial affairs of our organization under the leadership of our Chief Financial
Officer, Thomas Boyer. During the past year, they have rolled out a new lodge
and hall accounting system, Intacct, which will provide our lodges and halls a new
tool to effectively manage their financial affairs. Currently there are approximately
170 lodges/halls utilizing or testing Intacct and we expect that number to increase
significantly by the end of this calendar year.
You can be very proud of the work that has been done by all those
involved in the financial affairs of our fraternity. The detailed financial information
I am going to give you today is for a nine-month period from the start of this
current fiscal year, November 1, 2012, through July 31, 2013. I will compare that
information to the same period a year earlier. This report is already posted on
the Member Center under Forms/164th Annual Communication. It will continue
to be available to you until the official proceedings of this Communication
are published. Those proceedings will contain the customary audited financial
statements for the entire fiscal year.
It should be noted that this partial-year information has been prepared
internally by our fine financial staff and has not been audited.
As of July 31, 2013, your Grand Lodge had assets of $10,350,990 and
liabilities of $ $7,067,583 for Total Net Assets of $3,283,407. Total Net Assets
were 9.1% higher than at the end of our October 31, 2012 fiscal year.
Keep in mind that most of the assets you might attach to the California
Grand Lodge are not actually owned by the Grand Lodge, itself, and do not
appear in these numbers. I am referring to assets such as this facility, which is
owned by the California Masonic Memorial Temple, our homes in Union City
and Covina which are owned by the Masonic Homes of California, the Acacia
Creek community in Union City and the California Masonic Foundation - all
separate corporations.
The investment accounts of the Grand Lodge were up 14.3% for the
12 months ending July 31, 2013. The annualized return for the prior three-year
period was 9.5% and 4.7% annualized for the prior five year period.
Your Grand Lodge continues to operate in the black on a year-to-year
basis. For the nine months ending July 31, 2013, total income was $ 1,826,236
while total expenses were $1,653,656. This income was 3.6% higher than the
comparative period last year. Expenses for the nine-month period ending July 31,
2013 were 4.7% higher. This increase related to open positions in 2012 that are
now filled in 2013 as well as a 2.5% merit increase.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

91

While the Net Excess of income over expenses is $172,580, it should be
noted that approximately 30% of total year’s expenses are expected to occur in the
last three months of the fiscal year. The current projection is that the Grand Lodge
will end the fiscal year on October 31st with a modest surplus.
The nine month expenses were divided in the following manner: 18.8%
for fraternal matters (such as this Annual Communication, travel expenses of
elected and appointed Grand Lodge Officers, insurance for the constituent lodges
as well as other miscellaneous fraternal expenses), 22.9% for Appropriations and
Programs (such as Leadership Development programs, various lodge support
committees, the Freemason magazine and other Committees such as Policy,
Jurisprudence, Investment, Ritual and Trial Review), and 58.3 % for General
and Administrative items (such as salaries and benefits, accounting and auditing,
investment management fees, legal fees and general office operations),
These results reflect the concern and diligence that the Executive
Committee and the Grand Lodge financial staff bring to the monitoring of actual
income and expenses versus the budget. The numbers are compiled and studied
by all parties in great detail as the year progresses. The result is that each Grand
Master starts his year with a zero balance with only the budget for that year to
work with.
I would like to thank the many highly dedicated brothers who serve on
the various boards and committees of this Grand Lodge and its related entities for
the extraordinary amount of time, energy, dedication and hard work they devote
to the business and fraternal affairs of our California Masonic community. Please
seek them out and say “Thank You” for the work they do.
Under the capable leadership of our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful
Allan Casalou, our Grand Lodge staff performs exceptional service for your Grand
Lodge and remains committed to offering exceptional support to our lodges and
our membership. Our Grand Lodge organization and administration is the model
among sister Grand Lodges. Please join me in thanking them.
And finally, my brethren, I thank each of you for having allowed me to
work with you and for you during this past year. I have been honored to be a part
of the California Masonic Grand Lodge team.
Respectfully submitted,
A. Raymond Schmalz, Grand Treasurer
