Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present to you this, my sixth report, as your
Grand Secretary.
Lodge and Membership Information
As of today, there are 337 chartered lodges in our jurisdiction, including
one lodge under dispensation and five research lodges.
Our membership including Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons,
at the beginning of the fiscal year was 65,551. For the 2013 fiscal year, we had
2,392 gains, and 4,029 losses. The ending membership on June 30, 2013, was
63,546, which includes 8,471 Entered Apprentice Masons, 1,763 Fellow Craft
Masons and 53,312 Master Masons. Our database also includes 25,526 Masonic
widows. A more detailed report of membership activity, together with a number of
Lodge by-law amendments, life memberships, and veteran’s awards is included in
my written report to be distributed in the Proceedings.
Summary of Accomplishments
There were a number of accomplishments during the year and I would
like to mention a few of them today.
This year we introduced the Masonic Leadership Program. While
we have successfully tailored leadership and management programs to our
fraternity over the years, we began this year with the goal of demonstrating
that Freemasonry has a lot to offer in understanding leadership principles and
practices. The Masonic Leadership Program uses concepts from Freemasonry to
discuss leadership and develop leadership skills. The program is based on the idea
that leaders live their values. More than 1,000 lodge and Grand Lodge leaders
participated in the program this year and we are excited to carry this program
over into the 2014 leadership retreats. In additional to our staff, there was a team
of facilitators that led the retreats this year and I want to thank them for their
time and talent. These facilitators included Worshipful Brothers Brian Bezner,
Wes Daniels, Bruce Galloway, Eric Hatfield, Marc Newman, David Perry, Chris
Rucker, Gary Silverman, Jeff Wilkins and Jordon Yelinek.
In January we published a new applicant investigation program. In an
effort to provide applicants with a more meaningful introduction to the lodge and
to provide lodge investigators with effective tools for the applicant interview, the
new investigation program is designed to shed greater light on the applicant’s

96

Proceedings of the

character and his reasons for making the application. The new program also
provides the applicant with information about the lodge and our expectations for
membership. The program is integrated into iMember for easy use by the lodge.
An explanation of the new program and a guide for investigators is available on
the Member Center.
As the Grand Master announced, we are very proud to release the first
version of the online candidate education program. Combining text with videos,
exercises, and links to related material, the new program should provide a rich
educational experience for candidates and Masons who desire to further their
Masonic education. There were a number of brothers who contributed to the
success of this release. While I cannot mention them all today, I do want to thank
Brother Angel Alvarez-Mapp and Worshipful Brother Adam Kendall who led the
video creation and art curation for the program. I also want to thank our Deputy
Grand Master, Right Worshipful Brother John Cooper, and Past Grand Master,
Most Worshipful Brother R. Stephen Doan who wrote a majority of the material
used in the program.
This week we learned that the first issue of the Freemason magazine for
the new Grand Lodge year, which was supposed to be shipped from the printer
to the Post Office following this Annual Communication, was actually shipped
early this week and a number of our members received it before this weekend.
While shipping something early is not normally an error, in this case it was, and
I apologize for any confusion or misunderstanding this error might have caused.
I continue to be very proud of our communication strategies. As you
know, we publish six issues of the California Freemason magazine in print and in
digital formats, we publish 12 issues of the electronic newsletter “The Leader” and
we publish an annual report. We maintain several websites, and utilize Facebook,
Twitter, You Tube and Instagram to communicate with our members and the general
public. For years now, I have reported to you that we maintain a membership in
AMP -the Association of Media and Publishing. This association recognizes the
communications of non-profit membership organizations throughout the United
States including service organizations like Rotary, trade associations like the
American Bar Association, charities like Habitat for Humanity, university alumni
organizations, and others. AMP makes three awards in several categories using
Gold, Silver, and Bronze awards to designate the first, second, and third award.
This year, the Masons of California won four awards, two bronze, one silver, and
one gold.
•

The digital version of the Freemason magazine was named the third best
digital magazine among all the member organizations earning the bronze
award for best digital magazine.

•

Our video about the Masonic apron titled “Emblems of Innocence and
Honor” also won a bronze award for best feature video.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

97

•

The Freemason magazine won a silver award for best magazine column
for “This Too Shall Pass” – an article about Stockton and the Stockton
Masonic Temple.

•

And, the Freemason magazine won a gold award for the best single
topic issue for the August/September 2012 Issue on Freemasonry
and Religion.

There are many people involved in the communication efforts of our
Grand Lodge. I do want to thank Terry Mendez, our Chief Communications Officer
and our entire staff including all of the writers, designers, and photographers who
contribute to our work.
There are over 200 regular Grand Lodges in the world and there is a
conference of these Grand Lodges held every 18 months. The World Conference
of Regular Grand Lodges is held in different cities around the world. Much like the
Olympics, Grand Lodges present bids to host the World Conference. I was very
proud to represent our Grand Lodge at the last World Conference in November
and present our bid to host the World Conference in 2015. There were three
additional bids made by other Grand Lodges. It is with great pride that I report
that the delegates of the last World Conference unanimously accepted our bid and
the 14th World Conference of Regular Grand Lodges will be held right here in our
Memorial Temple in San Francisco during the third week of November, 2015.
This will be a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for you and all of our members to
meet with brothers from around the world. Promotion and registration materials
will be made available in the spring.
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges
It is my responsibility as the Grand Secretary to keep the Grand Master
informed on matters pertaining to the recognition of foreign Grand Lodges and
to present to you in the form of a motion the recognition of certain Grand Lodges
that meet our criteria therefore.
Section 409.010 of the California Masonic Code permits our Grand Lodge
to recognize any Grand Lodge that is regularly formed by lodges which trace their
origin to regular and legitimate Ancient Craft Masonry; hold undisputed sway as
the acknowledge sole or concurrent supreme power in Ancient Craft Masonry in
the territory in which they claim jurisdiction; confine their authority and exercise
thereof to the three degrees of Craft or Symbolic Masonry; and subscribe to the
General Regulation of Freemasonry.
We receive aid in the evaluation of Grand Lodges seeking recognition by
the Commission on Information for Recognition, a committee of the Conference
of Grand Masters of Masons of North America. We are honored in California that
our very own Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother William J. Bray III, is
a member of that commission.

98

Proceedings of the

One Grand Lodge has written to our Grand Lodge seeking
mutual recognition.
The Grand Lodge of Monaco
The Regular National Grand Lodge of the Principality of Monaco was
formed by seven lodges and consecrated on February 19, 2011, by the United
Grand Lodge of England in association with the United Grand Lodge of Germany
and the French National Grand Lodge.
It is the opinion of the Commission on Information for Recognition that
this Grand Lodge meets the requirements for recognition. Therefore, I move that
the Grand Lodge of California grant mutual recognition to the Grand Lodge of
Monaco. Motion ADOPTED.
As I conclude my report, I also wish to extend my appreciation and
gratitude to the 337 lodge Secretaries and 164 Assistant Secretaries in this
jurisdiction whose dedicated work is the backbone of our lodges and of our Grand
Lodge. I also wish to thank our Assistant Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors
who, in addition to their Ritual duties, work very diligently on a number of
administrative matters throughout the year.
I am blessed to work with a team of true professionals in our Grand
Lodge office all of whom care deeply about our fraternity and support our mission
with their dedicated service. I thank them all for their service and commitment.
Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother John
F. Lowe, for his continued support and good leadership. I consider it a privilege to
work so closely with our Grand Masters. I’m able to learn so much about them as
they work through the large number of opportunities and challenges that need to be
addressed each year. Grand Master Lowe has demonstrated outstanding leadership
during the year. He has opened the door to so many of our accomplishments this
year and he addressed every challenge with the wisdom and strength that is so
exemplary of our fraternity. Thank you, Most Worshipful, for your leadership and
your friendship.
And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work
with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

Appendix F

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

121

Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Our Code requires the Grand Lecturer to “Render to Grand Lodge, at
each Annual Communication, a full and detailed account of his services during
the year, and to set forth, with respect to ritual, the condition of the Lodges”.
Therefore, I offer the following report.
It has been a pleasure and a very high honor to serve you as Grand
Lecturer this year and it is a memory that I will cherish for the rest of my life.
In support of our Grand Master’s theme to think “Beyond The Lodge”
I have worked to remind our Brethren of the importance of thinking “beyond
the ritual” by teaching its rich history so we may be able to live and experience
each moment of our ritual so it remains relevant in our lives and makes us more
successful both as individuals and as lodges.
Our ritual developed as a means by which our ancient Brethren banded
together for protection and as a means to share their physical and moral skills with
their dearest friends, who, by virtue of membership, became their Brothers. These
shared physical and moral skills are everlasting, highly valued, and their relevancy
stands the test of time. This heritage allows us to participate in a shared experience
with the Brethren of our past thus forming an everlasting and universal bond of
Brotherly Love and fellowship that continues through eternity.
Regarding my service to you this past year - As I traveled and provided
ritual instruction, I stressed the importance of quality ritual and the need to pay
attention to its detail as a foundation upon which the ritual and administrative
culture of our lodges is built. When you are not steadfast and fail to maintain ritual
quality in your respective lodges your ritual work will fall to various levels of
embarrassment, which has a cancerous effect on your lodge’s culture. No matter
how well-meaning a Brother’s intent might be, the want of ritual excellence
is sufficient to render him ineffectual to his own development and service to
his lodge.
The following is a summary of my attempt to encourage our Brethren to
develop a lodge culture that takes ownership of their ritual and to do all within
their power to ensure high quality ritual performance.
First, this year started with an Assistant Grand Lecturer training day
whereby instruction was provided in the various ceremonies that involve Grand
Lodge Officers and included instruction in the institution of a new lodge,
constitution of a new lodge, mortgage burning ceremony and the cornerstone
ceremony. Additionally, the Grand Marshal was invited to attend this training
session to provide him with an opportunity to refine his new Grand Lodge
Officer duties.

122

Proceedings of the

Secondly, hard work with the Ritual Committee and the Grand Master’s
appointed Task Force on Ritual resulted in a document to resolve floor work
misunderstandings and cement our ritual into the future. To accomplish this task,
the Ritual Committee prepared a draft Ritual Floor Work Manual that includes
definitions, ritual tips, the jewel march, all three Degrees including their respective
proficiencies, the flag presentation, balloting, calling down and back up again, the
reception of a Grand Lodge Officer, calling to refreshment and returning to labor
from refreshment, commonly mispronounced and/or misunderstood words, and
ritual-related policy. Additionally, when completed online users will be able to
click on specific words and be directed to additional information and/or further
historical explanation.
When completed and approved by the Grand Master, the intent is to
share this Manual with every District Inspector with the proviso that they take
one year to critically review and use the Manual in order to discover any errors,
omissions or misunderstood instruction. At the end of the one-year review period
a final version will be adopted that will become the “official” ritual floor work
manual of California and made available to others who teach our ritual as an aid
to the memory.
The Manual’s preparation was a monumental task and could not have
been completed without the very detailed analysis and constructive review
provided the by following ritual experts: The current members of the Ritual
Committee (Worshipfuls Wes Daniels, Bruce Galloway, Jeff Wilkins, Ricky
Lawler, Lynn Wallingford, Cub Jack, Roy Pool, Frank Lee, Jim Kurupas, and
Doug Eichen) and their respective Inspectors, particularly Worshipfuls Max
Rush and Nicholas Mitchell, supported by former Assistant Grand Lecturers
Worshipfuls Jack McEnterfer, Dave Allmuth, and Chuck Jeronimo, and further
supported by the members of the ritual teams from the Stan Salter School of
Masonic Instruction and Division 8. On behalf of the Craft I thank you for your
outstanding collaborative efforts to prepare this gift to our Fraternity.
Thirdly, as a way to provide Inspectors with something to make their
District Officer Schools of Instruction more meaningful and relevant, a pilot
program was initiated whereby Inspectors and Lodge Masters may opt to have
quarterly ritual instruction at their respective lodges in lieu of the monthly unified
schools. Each quarter the Inspector would visit each Master’s lodge to watch as
the officers, under the supervision of the Officer’s Coach, exemplified one of the
three degrees with the Inspector, if necessary, providing additional instruction:
During the 1st Quarter each lodge would exemplify the 1st Degree; during the
2nd Quarter the 2nd Degree; during the 3rd Quarter the 3rd Degree, and during
the 4th Quarter the Installation and other administrative matters. In addition to
the quarterly ritual examinations the Inspector may have joint meetings of the
officers of the lodges in his District to maintain fellowship and to discuss mutual
administrative matters. This pilot program will operate for another year before
being critically reviewed.

123

The ritual condition of the Lodges in California - This year I supervised
two Inspector ritual conferences and 7 Master Mason ritual schools covering all
three degrees. During those ritual schools, I tried to instill into each lodge an
understanding of the need for our Brethren to pay attention to ritual detail and a
desire to take personal ownership of the quality of their ritual. Paying attention to
the detail allows each Brother to personally chisel out, build, and perfect his own
character, thus turning his personal rough ashlar into a perfect ashlar.
This year the Inspectors’ ritual conferences included a review of the
various Grand Lodge ceremonies that Inspectors are required to supervise.
Each of these instructional opportunities provided an opportunity to
gauge the quality and consistency of our ritual throughout the State. I must say
that work exemplified by the ritual teams assembled for each Master Masons’
School, as well as the work exemplified by the Inspectors during their ritual
conferences, was consistent with what has been taught by Past Grand Lecturers as
well as your current Grand Lecturer.

124

Proceedings of the

The quality of our ritual is in safe hands within our corps of Inspectors
and Assistant Grand Lecturers and is being taught in a very standard and consistent
manner by our officer’s coaches.
The evidence demonstrates that our members love and respect our ritual;
however, there still remain a few lodges whose members have allowed the spirit
of mediocrity to creep into their work. With those lodges it is obvious that they
have allowed a tradition of not paying attention to detail to become imbedded into
their lodge culture. To those lodges I strongly encourage each member to make an
effort to change the lodge culture by making a recommitment to pay attention to
detail and to take ownership of, and improve, the ritual experience. Such a change
in culture will lead to administrative improvement that creates opportunities
to improve relationships between the Brethren that will in turn inspire them to
recommend new members to the lodge and generate growth.

wish you continued success into the future.
In conclusion, there are three rules to obtaining quality ritual: The
first is “Repetition”, the second is “Repetition”, and the third is, you guessed it,
“Repetition. No amount of instruction by me, the Assistant Grand Lecturers, your
Inspector, or your Officers Coach can improve your ritual performance until you
and the Lodge members themselves make that all important choice to work as
a team to take ownership of the quality of the your work and through repetition
improve the ritual experience within your lodge.
Thank you for your support and confidence.

Grand Chaplain’s Message

by The Very Reverend Randall L. Brill
Most Worshipful Sir, Past Grand Masters, Distinguished and Honored
Guests, my fellow Grand Lodge Officers, and my Brothers:
On July 19, 1989, United Airlines flight 232, left Denver for Chicago.
I was booked on that flight and my suitcase was checked in. Not long after it
reached altitude, 232 lost an engine and all hydraulic controls. Attempting an
emergency landing in Sioux City, Iowa, the DC-10 fell short of the runway causing
it to tumble, break apart and burst into flames. For the next several days, every
television network would broadcast images of the plane literally cart wheeling
down the runway. Thanks to the heroism of the pilot and crew, 185 out of 285
lives were saved that day. This FedEx package contains what is left of the contents
of my suitcase. It was on flight 232. By the grace of God, I was not!
A very fortunate chain of events caused me to change flights to Chicago
and board another airplane that left just five minutes before 232’s departure. The
change was so sudden that I went to one airplane and my suitcase went to the
other. Although I have never personally seen it, I have been told that my name
appears on the passenger manifest for that flight. Colleagues waiting for my
arrival at my destination learned of the crash and were officially told by United
representatives that I was believed to be aboard 232 – disposition unknown. It
would take more time than we have this morning to describe all of the events that
followed; discovery of my safety by family and co-workers, lost luggage, and
even a period of denial that featured my attempts to make a near-death situation
humorous. Suffice it to say that it didn’t take long before reality set in and I found
myself wrestling with questions like why was I spared and why was I given a
second chance when a good number of my fellow travelers, victims of the same
flight delays that affected me, were aboard flight 232?
How would you feel if you narrowly escaped death and were given a
second chance at life? Most survivors immediately wonder why they were spared.
The answer they typically settle on is that there is something in this life that they
still have to accomplish. Then they begin the pursuit of the answer to the question,
what is it I have left to do? And, by the way, one not need have faced death to
ask that question.
What would you do? Would you seek a higher level of faith and
spirituality? Would you set your sights on some grand social or professional goal
that would bring you recognition? Would you seek to make yourself and those
around you happier with material wealth? Or would you make some substantial
charitable contribution that would make you noteworthy? Those possibilities
all focus on something grandiose that will enhance your own life and, when it

128

Proceedings of the

becomes obvious that such goals are out of reach and require more effort to attain
than you thought, one tends to let go of the quest and return to the same old
habits of living. UNLESS, unless there is a realization of something more subtle
and basic.
I struggled to make sense out of my narrow escape. It had to mean that
I indeed had something important yet to do in my life. I asked God and myself
all of the questions I have already mentioned and more. Only in hindsight can I
see possible answers: I rose to prominence in my profession and field of science;
I would eventually divorce and years later remarry; I received recognition for
serving my country in the Middle East; I became a Freemason and stand here in
front of you this morning in the midst of an amazing Masonic journey. Why did
I get a second chance? I am not certain but I can tell you what finally occurred to
me. It’s not about grandiose, significant accomplishments – those can’t be planned
or predicted with certainty anyway. It’s not even about changing my own life.
More importantly, I realized that it’s about how I might change the lives of others
without knowing it. It is about the little things we do that are spontaneous and
unplanned – and the one or more of those that may make a difference in someone
else’s life. In other words, it’s not about what happens in my life, it’s about what
happens in the lives of others around me!
We tend to overlook the fact that our actions and the words we speak are
witnessed and overheard by untold numbers of people, most of whom we are not
even aware; a friendly gesture, the touch of a caring hand, a smile, a hug, a favor
done, a compliment, a comment heard or an action seen by people around us we
don’t even know are there. Any one and all of those things have the potential to
change someone’s life without our ever knowing it. That may well be the reason
for getting a second chance: not a change in my life but in the life someone else
who would not be affected if I were not around. It is those little things we do that
have the greatest potential for fitting into God’s plans for ourselves and, more
importantly, for others.
In one way or another, whether it is through faith or inspiration from the
Supreme Being, we are all given second chances to pay attention to how we live.
Living a good life without expecting anything in return is what truly matters. To
be considerate, kind, and generous without seeking recognition, yet being aware
that our spontaneous words and actions may well affect others known or unknown
to us, should be one of our major concerns. And accepting the fact that we, each
one of us, are a small but important piece of a grand design is critical to any
second chances we may be fortunate enough to receive.
The Great Architect Himself has provided guidance to us in His Holy
Law; the writings that we Masonically value as our principle light. For example,
in Philippians we are clearly instructed, “Do nothing from selfishness or empty
conceit, but with humility of mind let each of you regard one another as more
important than himself; do not merely look out for your own personal interests,
but also for the interest of others” (Philippians 2:3-11).

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

129

Certainly Masonry provides the tools and knowledge that we can apply to
shape the way we live. Albert Pike in Morals and Dogma reminds us, “The word
well spoken, the deed fitly done, even by the feeblest or humblest, cannot help
but have their effect.” More to the point, every Mason present this morning has
heard these words: “To soothe the unhappy, to sympathize with their misfortunes,
to compassionate their miseries, and to restore peace to their troubled minds is
the great aim we have in view.” Has it occurred to you that you can satisfy that
charge simply by being aware of your daily words and actions – or, do I dare say,
by applying what our Craft teaches?
I submit to you that it’s not about your life or mine; it’s about the effect
we have on the lives of others whether we know what or who we have affected.
Every day represents another chance to make a difference. So embrace each day
that you are given, appreciate what God has provided, and put it to good purpose.
Evan Esar, an American humorist, nicely summarizes the sentiments
I’ve attempted to convey this morning, “We can’t do much about the length of our
lives, but we can do plenty about its width and depth.”
May the blessing of the Almighty be on you and yours today and always.

Grand Oration
Grand Master. Behold how good and how pleasant it is for Brethren
to dwell together in Unity. As we have traveled the length and breadth of our
State, celebrating anniversaries of Lodges so mature that a precious gemstone or
mineral cannot be ascribed to them, and forming new Lodges as a Masonic Oasis,
returning the light of our Craft to long forgotten places and bringing it to new
horizons, the beauty of Brotherly Love has been the constant connection. Behold
how good and how pleasant it is for Brethren to dwell together in Unity.
It is a particular honor to look out from this podium across the assembled
leaders of our Craft. There are men of every sect, creed and opinion in this room,
who have set aside their daily toils, to join in this work we have at hand for the
benefit of all Masons, including those who have gone this way before us and those
who have yet to take their first step in Freemasonry.
Earlier this year, I was privileged to attend the awarding of a 50 year pin
to a Brother of a Lodge in Connecticut, and in the ceremony it said:
Each Mason gives of his substance; many give also of their time; while
others add loyalty and steadfast devotion. But to all of us, our gentle
Craft gives far more than we could give it in a lifetime of service. Today
we pay tribute to the Fraternity which opened its portals to each of us,
and made it possible for each of us to build our lives on the sublime
principles it inculcates.
Let us celebrate that Fraternity now. In this room there are Lodges that
take every shape and form. There are social Lodges, there are philanthropic and
service oriented Lodges, there are academically bent Lodges and there are family
oriented Lodges. There are Lodges built to fit each and every one of us. Though
what causes us to rise beyond being a simple grouping of men into something
greater, something beyond ourselves, is our ritual, it is our common connection to
the past, and though it, to the future.
A basic problem which has plagued mankind for centuries has been the
problem of communication, how we pass down to others those things which have
been the most vital and relevant to our lives. In every age individual men have
encouraged a transcending experience which cuts to the depth of their being,
reconciles them to other men, and gives them courage to suffer adversity… such
has been called the religious experience, oneness or union with God. But there
has always been a great difficulty in communicating this experience to others,
for it lies outside the context of everyday experience and defies the limitations
of language.

134

Proceedings of the

Thus, centuries ago men began trying to preserve this transcending
experience for future generation in the form of a stylized drama which took the
form of a secret ritual, in which the older members of the community, through the
enactment of a mythical story, recalling the heroic acts of equally mythic heroes,
transmitted the ancient mysteries to younger generations. Through experience the
elders knew that their secret rituals, if properly conducted, possessed a tremendous
power to re-create religious experiences within the heart of the novice. Through
ritualistic employment of drama and symbol, the novice under ideal conditions
was brought to a higher level of consciousness, which enabled him to find
validation for his own life within the context of the community or brotherhood
and to see his life as a part of a divine plan.
Fully integrated into the secret mysteries, the novice could at last find
meaning where head once known uncertainty; he could at last see purpose and
order, where he had once only known confusion and chaos.
The power of our ritual lays in its dramatic quality, not as dry, lifeless
words written on a page, but rather as a living thing, a liturgy, work that brothers
do together, as a reflection of their common aspirations as a Lodge, together with
their singular aspirations as Brethren. By means of dramatic action ritualistic
dialogue, systems of values, symbols and allegory, we recreated momentarily
our own exalted vision of human perfection, that which elevates us out of
commonplace desires into the more noble and godlike realms of our nature.
The whole ritual is built to produce a sensory experience upon the viewer
as well as the participant: an experience which appeals to the mind as well as to
the emotions and cuts to the depths of all levels of human consciousness. Not only
should the initiate see and hear, but he must also feel.
Though all the words, movements and sounds be technically perfect,
nothing is more important in producing this emotional feeling than an absolute
sincerity on the part of the Brethren conferring the degree, a sincerity that only
comes from a deeply held belief and conviction in the words that they are speaking
and in that degree which they are conferring. Unless we are moved, the initiate
will not be.
At its heart and best our Craft is a utopian experiment based on certain
idealistic principles found in our degrees. The selective banding together of men
who learn from each other, and ultimately rely upon each other is a seemingly
hopeless task as witnessed by the recurring quarrels, feuds and rivalries which
come about in the Lodge.
Yet, despite our individual collective shortcomings, and despite the
sometimes disappointments of Lodge life, the fraternity has continued to provide
a profound and lasting experience for generations of Brethren. And though we
may often think of the Lodge simply as a place where good times may be had
and good friends may be found, on certain occasional nights of every month, by

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

135

means of an archaic ceremony enacted with great secrecy, we are transported out
of the realm of everyday experience and into a shadowy, mystical worlds of pomp
and splendor. Here, once again, through symbol and allegory we catch a glimpse
of mans eternal potentiality. We learn the genuine basis of the Craft’s existence,
and we hear the familiar vows that first enabled us to call each other brother. Into
our apathy and into our complacency the Craft comes, binding us back to our
original purpose from which we often stray. It is this recreation of that utopian
vision which lifts us up out of the profane and commonplace, restoring in us a
sense of unity.
There was an additional line from that 50 year ceremony in Connecticut
that personally touched me:
May the joy of this moment abide with you always, and may
you ever stand as you once stood in the northeast corner -- a
just and upright Mason, worthy to be known as a son of God.
It is a striking charge that calls us forward, to be above reproach, to
act so that we have no cause to be ashamed of ourselves. Let us, each one of us,
commit in our hearts to being an agent of profound change in the world, through
the collective actions our Craft and our own endeavors, and hold ourselves to
that charge.
Our 33rd President of the United States, and the 97th Grand Master of
Masons in Missouri, Bro. Harry Truman once said “We represent a fraternity
which believes in justice and truth and honorable action in your community...
men who are endeavoring to be better citizens... to make a great country greater.
This is the only institution in the world where we can meet on the level all sorts of
people who want to live rightly.”
Through our concerted acts we bring light into the world, through
philanthropy such as Raising a Reader, we are improving the lives of children,
and through them our communities and providing for a brighter future for us
all. However, the charges given to us speak not only to concerted acts, but
individual ones.
We must constantly ask ourselves if tomorrow ceased to exist, would
anyone know the difference. We must, each one of us, personally, seek to leave
a positive change in the world, and find daily inspiration. Or, in the words of
Winston Churchill, “You make a living by what you get. You make a life by what
you give.”

136

Proceedings of the

In the years that follow, when this Annual Communication is called
together and we have each long passed the mortal veil, may those who follow
us gather here again, having committed ourselves today to making a profound
difference in the world around us, that they may say we were are all worthy to be
known as sons of God.
God bless you all, God bless these United States, and may we always
behold how good and how pleasant it is for Brethren to dwell together in Unity.
Respectfully submitted,
Jordan T. Yelinek, Grand Orator

Grand Master’s Recommendation
Grand Master Lowe’s Recommendation No. 1
Permits a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons to Call Up to a
Higher Degree for the Purpose of Examination
The requirement to hold Stated Meetings in the First Degree denies us
the option of conducting candidate examinations in the Second and Third Degrees
at a Stated Meeting. To offer Lodges this option, it is my recommendation that
Lodges be allowed to call up from the First to either the Second or Third Degrees
for examinations at a Stated Meeting. However, just as our law currently limits
the purpose for which a Lodge may be called down, my recommendation would
allow a Lodge to call up for examination only. If this recommendation is adopted,
you could not call up to confer a degree, just as you cannot now call down to
confer a degree.
If you adopt this recommendation, the Code will be changed to allow a
lodge to call up to a higher degree for the purpose of examination.
The Monitor and Officers Manual will be amended to add the necessary
provisions to call up. These are based on the existing provisions used to call down.
Brethren who are not entitled to be present in a lodge of a higher degree will be
excused before the lodge is called up and admitted back into the lodge after the
lodge is called back to the first degree.
The Grand Secretary shall make appropriate modifications to the table
of contents and pagination of the Monitor and Officers Manual should this
recommendation be adopted.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
From the earliest days of Masonry in California, Lodges had the ability
to conduct examinations in the Candidate’s Lecture in any of the three degrees at
a Stated Meting, since business was conducted in the Master Mason degree. When
Grand Lodge adopted a resolution at the 2012 Annual Communication required
Stated Meetings to be conducted in the Entered Apprentice degree, the ability to
examine candidates in the Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees was lost, since
a Lodge, once opened, cannot be called up to a higher degree.
The prohibition on “calling up” derives in part from the concern that a
Brother Mason who is properly entitled to attend the degree in which the Lodge
is opened might inadvertently be present when the Lodge is a labor on a degree to
which he is not entitled. It is therefore the responsibility of the Master to ensure
that such Brethren retire from the Lodge before calling up to a higher degree.

140

Proceedings of the

This Grand Master’s Recommendation would restore the ability
of a Lodge to examine candidates in any of the three degrees by allowing a
Lodge to call up to a higher degree solely for the purpose of examination.
Masons in attendance who have not received that degree would have to retire
until the examination was completed and the Lodge called back to the Entered
Apprentice degree.
This recommendation is consistent with the policy and general purposes
of this Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
As indicated by the Grand Master, the requirement to hold Stated Meetings
in the First Degree denies us the option of conducting candidate examinations in
the Second and Third Degrees at a Stated Meeting. This recommendation resolves
the issue by allowing the Master the ability to call up to a higher degree solely
for the purpose of conducting such examination. The Ritual Committee supports
this recommendation.
Recommendation APPROVED.

Carry-Over from 2012 Annual Communication
Resolution No. 12-02
Requires the Senior Warden-Elect to Qualify in the Master’s Work and Lecture
of Both the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the conditions necessary to
install the Senior Warden by requiring him to be proficient in the Master’s work
and lecture of both the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Resolution No. 2008-05 attempted to clarify the conditions
necessary to install the Master and Senior Warden by requiring each officer to
know the work and lectures of their current position as well as the Master’s work
and lectures of the previous office; and
WHEREAS, Resolution No. 2008-05 as adopted omitted the requirement
for the Senior Warden to be proficient in the Master’s work and lecture of the
Entered Apprentice Degree;
WHEREAS, qualification consistency should be the goal for
advancement; and
WHEREAS, this resolution is a house cleaning measure meant to
eliminate confusion.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.530 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.530. CONDITIONS TO INSTALLATION OF THE SENIOR
WARDEN-ELECT.
Before a Senior Warden‑elect can be installed, there shall be presented to the
Installing Officer a Certificate of Qualification of the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant
Grand Lecturer of the division in which his Lodge is situated, or the Inspector of
the district in which his Lodge is situated, certifying that:
A.

He has personally examined the Senior Warden‑elect and that he is
qualified to give the Senior Warden’s work of the Entered Apprentice,
Fellow Craft and Master Mason Degrees, and the Master’s work and
lectures of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees;

B.

He has received a Certificate of Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture of
the Master Mason Degree; and

C.

He is proficient in those portions of this Code that relate to the government
of a Lodge.

142

Proceedings of the

Immediately after the installation, the Installing Officer shall endorse the Senior
Warden’s Certificate of Qualification and forward it to the Grand Secretary.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the section of the
California Masonic Code involving the qualifications of the Senior Warden.
Prior to the adoption of the Fourth Edition of the California Masonic
Code in 2006, section 25080–A required the Senior Warden elect to be proficient
in “the work and lectures of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees.”
That language was carried over into the new code in section 805.530. In 2008,
section 805.530 was amended to make it clear that the Senior Warden-elect had to
be proficient in the Master’s work and lecture of the Fellow Craft degree as well
as the Senior Warden’s work of all three degrees. However, Resolution 08-05
inadvertently deleted the long-standing requirement that the Senior Warden-elect
also be proficient in the lecture of the Entered Apprentice degree.
Resolution 2012-02 corrects the Code by making it clear that a Senior
Warden-elect must be proficient in the Senior Warden’s work of all three degrees
as well as the lectures of both the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees.
It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that the Senior Warden
be proficient in the work as well as the lectures of the Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft degrees so that he could, if the need arose, take the chair of the
Junior Warden for the presentation of degrees. This Resolution makes it clear that
the Senior Warden elect must be so qualified.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 12-03
Withdrawals From Life Membership Funds
The proponents of this Resolution seek to modify how withdrawals are taken from
a Lodge Life Membership Fund.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, we have not been consistent as to the manner and timing of
a Lodge’s withdrawals from a Life Membership Fund pursuant to Section 809.150
of the California Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, there should be a consistent approach to such
withdrawals; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

143

WHEREAS, some Lodges have not withdrawn the permissible amount
of interest and dividends from the Life Membership Fund on an annual basis; and
WHEREAS, Lodges which have failed to make the permitted
withdrawals should not be penalized if the law in this area is modified.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.150 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.150. LIFE MEMBERSHIP FUND.
The original amounts paid for life memberships shall be forever kept and
maintained held as and for a separate and permanent Life Membership Fund. A
Lodge may invest its Life Membership Fund as provided in Section 809.130 of
this Code, if such investments are kept separate and apart from all other Lodge
assets. Only interest or dividends paid in cash on the Life Membership Fund
shall be available for general Lodge use. Interest and dividends received during
a calendar year must be withdrawn on or before December 31st of the following
calendar year. Otherwise, they shall be added to principal and may not thereafter
be withdrawn.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that, if there is any interest or dividends
paid in cash on a Lodge’s Life Membership Fund during the two complete fiscal
years ending prior to the adoption of this Resolution which has not previously
been withdrawn for general Lodge use, the Lodge may withdraw such amounts
for general Lodge use by December 31 of the calendar year of the adoption of
this Resolution.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that, should this resolution and one
or more of Resolutions 12-04, 12-07 and 12-08 be adopted, the modifications of
Section 809.150 of the California Masonic Code as enacted by this Resolution
12-03 shall be repealed.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Initially, Resolution No. 12-03 was designed to clarify the fact that any
income from life membership funds that was not used in the year it was earned
to be considered principal, and those dollars could not be used in future years.
Up until then, some Lodges viewed any income that was ever earned would be
available for Lodge expenditure indefinitely. In order to provide Lodges with a
final opportunity to withdraw earned income that had not been used in the previous
two ears, part of Resolution 12-03 provided a grace period for Lodges to withdraw
that money. The clarification about unused funds becoming principal was passed
as part of another Resolution in 2012. However, Resolution 12-03 was carried

144

Proceedings of the

over. Passage of this Resolution now will permit Lodges to have until December
31, 2013 to withdraw unused income from the past two years. Beginning in 2014,
only monies earned in the one eligible year will be available to the Lodges.
It is the policy of this Grand Lodge to permit changes and clarifications
in the manner in which life membership funds are administered and also to avoid
excess hardship when those policies are changed.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 12-04
Requires Life Membership Funds to be Invested For Total Return and
Establishes Rules For Life Membership Gifts and Contributions
The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide clarity and direction as to how
a Life Membership Fund should be managed.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 809.150 of the California Masonic Code
specifically allows a Life Membership Fund to be invested for “total return,”
in a like manner as all other Lodge funds, according to the rules of Section
809.130; and
WHEREAS, the “interest or dividends paid in cash” clause does not
adequately include all the permissible types of investments and withdrawals as
provided for in Section 809.130 of the California Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, many Lodges are under the incorrect assumption that Life
Membership Funds should be invested only in very safe vehicles such as checking,
savings, money market or certificates of deposit accounts, which do not provide
adequate returns to allow the Fund to keep pace with inflation or provide growth,
let alone replace the dues income from a member or even cover the expenses of
the Grand Lodge Per Capita Tax; and
WHEREAS, the “original amounts . . . shall be forever kept and
maintained” clause was never meant to be an obstacle to prudent investment as
provided for in Section 809.130 of the California Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, “forever kept and maintained” does not require that
investments be made with a guarantee of retaining principal; and
WHEREAS, the idea that the investment of the Life Membership Fund
must be kept separate and apart from all other Lodge assets does not mean that
the fund must be invested differently from other Lodge assets, only that it must be
segregated and invested separately from other Lodge assets; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

145

WHEREAS, the contract entered into between the purchasing member
and the Lodge at the time of purchase of a life membership is simple: the purchasing
member pays the Lodge a fixed sum and the Lodge promises the purchaser that he
will never again pay dues to that Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the Lodge promises that the member will never again be
required to pay dues in that Lodge even if the assets in the Life Membership Fund
are no longer sufficient to pay his dues.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.150 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.150. LIFE MEMBERSHIP FUND.
The original amounts paid for life memberships shall be forever kept and
maintained as and for a separate and permanent Life Membership Fund. A Lodge
may invest its Life Membership Fund as provided in Section 809.130 of this
Code, if such investments are kept separate and apart from all other Lodge assets.
Only interest or dividends paid in cash on the Life Membership Fund shall be
available for general Lodge use.
A.

All amounts paid for a life membership shall constitute a permanent Life
Membership Fund, which shall be segregated into one or more accounts
which are separate from all other Lodge funds, investments and assets.

B.

A Lodge may only invest its Life Membership Fund as provided in
Section 809.130 of this Code. However, all investments of the Life
Membership Fund described in Section 809.130.B of this Code must
be conservative growth investments which are designed for total return
(defined as any investment returns, including capital gains/appreciation
and losses/depreciation – realized or unrealized – and all dividends
and interest).
A Lodge’s Life Membership Fund may not be used to secure or fund any
loan to a Lodge or Hall Association, nor may it be used as collateral for a
mortgage or promissory note to or for the benefit of any entity or person.

C.

A Lodge may withdraw the income from its Life Membership Fund for
the general use of the Lodge at any time. For this purpose, income means
all interest and dividends received in cash with respect to investments
held as part of the Life Membership Fund. However, no Lodge is
obligated to take withdrawals from its Life Membership Fund. Interest
and dividends received during a calendar year must be withdrawn on or
before December 31st of the following calendar year. Otherwise, they
shall be added to principal and may not thereafter be withdrawn.

D.

A Lodge purchasing a life membership for the retiring Master as
provided in Section 809.550.D of this Code must transfer the total
purchase price of the life membership from its general funds to its Life
Membership Fund.

146

Proceedings of the

E.

A life membership may be purchased as a memorial at any time for a
Master Mason who, at the time of his death, was a member in good
standing of the Lodge. The purchase price for such life membership shall
be paid in full at the time of purchase and calculated in accordance with
Section 809.320 of this Code and the current life membership plan of
the Lodge. If a Lodge uses the plan described in Section 809.320.B, the
purchase price shall be calculated by using the age of the member at the
time of his death.

F.

Nothing in this Code shall prevent any person from making voluntary
contributions to the Life Membership Fund.

G.

A Life Membership Fund, once established, may never be dissolved
or combined with general Lodge funds, even if there may be no life
members currently living or if further sales of life memberships have
been discontinued.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.320 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.320. LIFE MEMBERSHIP.
A Lodge may adopt a standing resolution providing for a life membership plan,
which shall forever exempt a member making the required payment into the plan
from the payment of dues in the Lodge. The resolution may be adopted, amended
or revoked at any Stated Meeting by a majority vote of the members present.
Any such action must be presented, in writing, at a preceding Stated Meeting and
written notice must be given to each Lodge member setting forth the text of the
proposed action and the date of the Stated Meeting at which the vote is to be taken.
The plan must provide that a life membership shall be granted upon payment of:
A.

A sum of money which is not less than 20.83 times the Lodge’s annual
dues at the time of purchase of the life membership; or

B.

A sum of money equal to the Lodge’s annual dues at the time of purchase
of the life membership multiplied by the factor indicated opposite the
member’s age in the following schedule:
Age 49 and under, 21 times annual dues;
50 to 54 inclusive, 19 times annual dues;
55 to 59 inclusive, 17 times annual dues;
60 to 64 inclusive, 14 times annual dues; and
65 and over, 11 times annual dues.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

147

The resolution shall take effect only upon its approval by the Grand Master.
The Secretary shall send to each life member at his last known address, annually,
a Life Membership Dues Card for the next calendar year.
A life membership is an executed contract requiring the consent of the Lodge and
the life member to rescind it.
The Grand Secretary shall provide the form of contract to be used by the Lodge
when a life membership is purchased (other than as a memorial). Such contract
must be signed by the member for whom the life membership is being purchased,
the Lodge Master and the Lodge Secretary, affixed with the seal of the Lodge. The
original shall be kept as part of the member’s permanent membership record. A
copy of the signed contract shall be provided to the member.
A life member who has been suspended or expelled and who shall thereafter
become restored or elected to membership in a Lodge in which a life membership
was once held shall also be restored as a life member of that Lodge.

Resolution No. 12-07
Requires Life Membership Funds be Invested For Total Return and
Allows Annual Withdrawals of Up to Four Percent of the Three Year
Average Fund Balance
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow each Lodge to invest its Life
Membership Fund for total return and withdraw annually four percent of the three
year average fund balance.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge to invest
the funds of the Grand Lodge of California in conservative investment instruments
and to allow its constituent Lodges to invest their funds in like manner; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California and its various entities
– including the Masonic Homes of California and the California Masonic
Foundation – invest their funds conservatively for total return; and
WHEREAS, conservative investments yield conservative, reliable and
profitable returns which allow for growth and inflation when prudently managed
over a long-term investment strategy; and
WHEREAS, it is desirable for Lodges to develop a long-term investment
strategy for their Life Membership Funds to keep pace with annual dues, pay the
Grand Lodge Per Capita Tax, account for inflation and provide for growth; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

149

WHEREAS, it is reasonable that a Lodge should be able to budget its
income from investments based on a steady percentage rather than the unknown
amount of dividends and interest which can vary widely.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.150 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.150. LIFE MEMBERSHIP FUND.
The original amounts paid for life memberships shall be forever kept and
maintained as and for a separate and permanent Life Membership Fund. A Lodge
may invest its Life Membership Fund as provided in Section 809.130 of this
Code, if such investments are kept separate and apart from all other Lodge assets.
Only interest or dividends paid in cash on the Life Membership Fund shall be
available for general Lodge use.
A.

All amounts paid for a life membership shall constitute a permanent Life
Membership Fund, which shall be segregated into one or more accounts
which are separate from all other Lodge funds, investments and assets.

B.

A Lodge may only invest its Life Membership Fund as provided in
Section 809.130 of this Code. However, all investments of the Life
Membership Fund described in Section 809.130.B of this Code must
be conservative growth investments which are designed for total return
(defined as any investment returns, including capital gains/appreciation
and losses/depreciation – realized or unrealized – and all dividends
and interest).
A Lodge’s Life Membership Fund may not be used to secure or fund any
loan to a Lodge or Hall Association, nor may it be used as collateral for a
mortgage or promissory note to or for the benefit of any entity or person.

C.

A Lodge may make withdrawals from its Life Membership Fund for the
general use of the Lodge in the following manner only:
1.

The December 31st value of the Lodge’s Life Membership Fund
for each of the prior three years shall be averaged together. The
maximum allowable withdrawal during the calendar year shall
be 4.0% of that averaged value, except as follows:
a.

If the Life Membership Fund of a Lodge has existed
for less than three complete calendar years, but for at
least one complete calendar year, the December 31st
value for each year in which the Fund was in existence
shall be averaged together. The maximum allowable
withdrawal during the calendar year shall be 4.0% of
that averaged value; and

150

Proceedings of the
b.

If the Life Membership Fund of a Lodge was created
in the prior calendar year, the maximum allowable
withdrawal during the calendar year shall be 4.0%
of the value on December 31st of the prior calendar
year; and

c.

If the Life Membership Fund of a Lodge was created
during the current calendar year, no withdrawals may
be made during the calendar year;

2.

Lodge withdrawals from its Life Membership Fund during each
calendar year may be made in one or more increments, provided
that the total withdrawal for the calendar year does not exceed
the maximum allowable withdrawal as calculated in paragraph
1 above. If a Lodge fails to withdraw any or all of the amount to
which it would have otherwise been entitled during a calendar
year, then it shall be prohibited from taking that withdrawal in
any subsequent year; and

3.

Permissible withdrawals under this section shall be transferred
to the Lodge’s bank or other investment accounts for the general
use of the Lodge.

The Grand Secretary shall provide the Lodges with a form which may be
used to make the calculations described above.
No Lodge is obligated to take withdrawals from its Life
Membership Fund.

Masonic Code made by the foregoing resolution become part of the Ordinances
on the January 1st following their adoption.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that, should two or all of Resolutions
12-04, 12-07 and 12-08 be adopted, the Committee on Jurisprudence be authorized
to letter the paragraphs of Section 809.150 of the California Masonic Code
sequentially as the committee shall determine.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify how each Lodge may
invest its Life Membership Fund for total return and withdrawal annually of up
to four percent of the three year average fund balance. This proposal would also
clarify the definition of investments, which may be unclear in the California
Masonic Code at the present. This revision provides that all investments of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

151

Life Membership Fund as described in CMC section 809.130 must be conservative
growth investments which are designed for total return which is defined as any
investment returns, including capital gains/appreciation and losses/depreciation realized or unrealized - and all dividends and interest.
The proponents also highly encourage Lodges to develop a long-term
investment strategy for their Life Membership Fund to keep pace with annual
dues, pay the Grand Lodge Per Capita Tax, account for inflation and provide for
growth in the Fund over the long term.
The proponents of this Resolution recognize that interest or dividends
may be inadequate for the needs of the Lodge, particularly in the periods of
financial uncertainty. The proposed revision of CMC section 809.150 would
allow the Lodge to know specifically, at the start of the Masonic Year, how much
money would be available from the Life Membership Fund. This rate is the same
as Grand Lodge employs.
This Resolution does not change the provision that a Lodge may never
access the original amounts paid for life memberships.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Investments:
This Resolution underscores the importance of investing Life
Membership Funds for long-term growth of capital and provides for a method
distribution more appropriate for an investment of this nature. This is consistent
with Section 809.130.B of the Code, which states that investments must be made
in conservative growth investments that are designed for total return.
While the resolution does not require a lodge to make annual withdrawals,
it does limit the annual withdrawals to 4% of the rolling three-year average. There
is no make-up provision for missed distributions. The Investment Committee
believes this is prudent investment practice, as it allows investments to b made in
long term investment vehicles, including appropriate non-dividend paying stocks
that allow the principal of the Life Membership Fund to grow over time, without
aggressively drawing down principal.
The Grand Lodge Investment Committee recommends adoption of
Carryover Resolution No. 12-07.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 12-09
Allows a Member to Transfer His Life Membership

The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the transfer of a life membership
between two Constituent Lodges.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it is unfair that dues-paying members of a Lodge may
transfer their memberships to another Lodge in this Jurisdiction without penalty,
but life members who wish to do so would be penalized by either having to
resume paying dues in his new Lodge or purchase another life membership in his
new Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the purpose of a life membership often is to avoid paying
dues thereafter; and
WHEREAS, in today’s mobile society it is not unusual for members to
relocate to an area which is a long distance from their Lodge and they desire to be
a member in the new area; and
WHEREAS, transferability would not be detrimental to the Lodge to
which a member wishes to transfer; and
WHEREAS, a refund of life membership dues is not available now
upon transferring to another Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that section 809.320 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.320. LIFE MEMBERSHIP.
A Lodge may adopt a standing resolution providing for a life membership plan,
which shall forever exempt a member making the required payment into the plan
from the payment of dues in the Lodge. The resolution may be adopted, amended
or revoked at any Stated Meeting by a majority vote of the members present.
Any such action must be presented, in writing, at a preceding Stated Meeting and
written notice must be given to each Lodge member setting forth the text of the
proposed action and the date of the Stated Meeting at which the vote is to be taken.
The plan must provide that a life membership shall be granted upon payment of:
A.

A sum of money which is not less than 20.83 times the Lodge’s annual
dues at the time of purchase of the life membership; or

B.

A sum of money equal to the Lodge’s annual dues at the time of purchase
of the life membership multiplied by the factor indicated opposite the
member’s age in the following schedule:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

153

Age 49 and under, 21 times annual dues;
50 to 54 inclusive, 19 times annual dues;
55 to 59 inclusive, 17 times annual dues;
60 to 64 inclusive, 14 times annual dues; and
65 and over, 11 times annual dues.
The resolution shall take effect only upon its approval by the Grand Master.
The Secretary shall send to each life member at his last known address, annually,
a Life Membership Dues Card for the next calendar year.
A life membership is an executed contract requiring the consent of the Lodge and
the life member to rescind it. A life member has no interest in the Lodge’s Life
Membership Fund, except in the case of a rescission of his life membership with
his consent and the consent of the Lodge or as elsewhere provided in this Code.
Any other provision of this Code to the contrary notwithstanding, a life member
of a Constituent Lodge who is a member of another Constituent Lodge which then
offers life memberships may elect to transfer his interest in the first Lodge Life
Membership Fund to the Life Membership Fund of the second Lodge. The life
member’s interest in the first Lodge’s Life Membership Fund shall be equal to the
lesser of the original sum of money paid to purchase his life membership or his
share of the fair market value of such Lodge’s Life Membership Fund at the time
of his election to membership in the second Lodge, as determined by the Grand
Treasurer. In making this determination, the Grand Treasurer shall compute the
interest of each living life member in the first Lodge’s Life Membership Fund and
the interest of the first Lodge in it, on a just and equitable basis. If such member’s
interest in the first Lodge’s Life Membership Fund is less than the current cost
of a life membership in the second Lodge, he must pay the difference within 60
days of the notice of its determination in order for the transfer of that amount to
be effective.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that, should two or all of Resolutions
12-04, 12-06 and 12-09 be adopted, the Committee on Jurisprudence be authorized
to arrange Section 809.320 of the California Masonic Code by paragraphs and
subparagraphs, lettered and numbered as appropriate, as and to the extent that the
committee shall determine.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the transfer of a Life
Membership between two Constituent Lodges. Presently it is not possible
to transfer such membership so a life member who wishes to do so would be

154

Proceedings of the

penalized by either having to resume paying dues in his new Lodge or purchase
another life membership in his new Lodge. The proponents propose a procedure
whereby the transfer of membership may be made.
Today, we have a very mobile society so it is not unusual for a member
to relocate to an area which may be a considerable distance from his Lodge, and
he is desirous of becoming a member in his new area. This proposal provides a
procedure by which he may do so and specifies what the transferring member
must pay if his interest in the first Lodge’s Life Membership Fund is less than the
current cost of a life membership in the second Lodge.
However, this proposed legislation would permit a member to
unilaterally transfer his life membership without the consent of his Lodge. The
life membership is a contract between the member and his Lodge, and it takes
both parties to a contract to effect a rescission. In addition, once a life membership
is purchased, the funds belong to the Lodge in perpetuity, and the member has no
interest therein.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 12-16
Requires Biographies of Candidates in Grand Lodge Elections
The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide a procedure for Grand Lodge
elective officer nominations from the floor.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Sections 404.420 and 404.430 of the California Masonic
Code specify that when recommendations for election to the offices of Junior Grand
Warden, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer are distributed, a
biographical sketch is attached only for the recommendee for election as Junior
Grand Warden; and
WHEREAS, only the Junior Grand Warden has his biographical sketch
read at Annual Communication; and
WHEREAS, a nominee for any of the elected offices may be made from
the floor; and
WHEREAS, the members of Grand Lodge cannot be expected to make
informed decisions if they do not know the qualifications of multiple nominees.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 404.410 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

155

§404.410. ELECTED OFFICERS.
The Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens, Grand Treasurer, Grand
Secretary, and Grand Lecturer shall be elected by written ballot as the final item
of business before the installation of said officers at each Annual Communication.
A majority of the votes cast shall be necessary for an election. Grand Lodge,
by unanimous consent, may permit any designated officer to cast the ballot for
Grand Lodge.
Each recommendee for election to any Grand Lodge office shall provide his
biographical sketch to the Grand Secretary no less than two weeks prior to the
start of Annual Communication. Any other member desiring to be nominated for
election as a Grand Lodge officer may provide his biographical sketch to the Grand
Secretary no less than two weeks prior to the start of Annual Communication.
Nominations for election to any Grand Lodge office shall include only the name
and current title of the nominee. At the conclusion of the nomination process
for each elective office, if there are multiple nominees, the Grand Orator shall
read the biographical sketch submitted for each nominee, if received by him at
least two weeks prior to the start of Annual Communication, in the order of their
nominations. The biographical sketch of the Junior Grand Warden shall be read by
the Grand Orator whether or not there are multiple nominees. The Grand Orator
shall read only the facts from each biographical sketch. If the Grand Secretary did
not receive a biographical sketch for a nominee by the required date, the vote shall
be taken without reading a biographical sketch for that nominee.
Each elective officer shall be installed before the close of the Annual
Communication and shall serve until the installation of his successor, subject to
Section 404.510. This installation may be public or private at the option of the
incoming Grand Master.
If an elective officer is unable to be present, due to circumstances beyond his
control, he may be installed by the Grand Master at an appropriate place, with
such ceremony as deemed proper by the Grand Master, as soon as practicable
not to exceed 60 days. If the elective officer is not installed within 60 days, the
office shall be declared vacant and the Grand Master may appoint any member of
Grand Lodge to fill the vacant elective office temporarily or for the remainder of
the Grand Lodge year.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution 12-16 seeks to amend Section 404.410 of our California
Masonic Code to provide a procedure for open nominations and for biographical
sketches to be provided for all elected positions of the Grand Lodge.

156

Proceedings of the

CMC Section 404.420 specifies that the residency of the Junior Grand
Elect shall alternate between the north and the south. This requirement is not
addressed in this open nomination process. Also, during the nomination of the
Junior Grand Warden, his biographical sketch is read by the Grand Secretary.
Although not specifically stated in the California Masonic Code, it has been the
practice of our Grand Master, during elections, to ask for “any other nominations.”
This is consistent with Robert’s Rules of Order, Chapter 12.
It is the policy of our Grand Lodge to provide as much information as
possible to the Craft before they elect a Grand Lodge officer.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 12-18
Requires Member Consent to Publish Personal Information to the Public
The proponents of this Resolution seek to require a member to give his consent
before his personal information may be published to the public.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, we live in an age of internet connectivity that presents
threats including identity theft; and
WHEREAS, personal information about ourselves, combined with our
commitment to aide one another, could when injected into the public domain
present an enticing target for criminals and con artists; and
WHEREAS, Freemasons are still persecuted in parts of the world and
some must travel to those places; and
WHEREAS, many members are law enforcement or correctional
officers whose identity, contact information and residences if know by criminals
may make them and their families targets of aggression and criminal acts by
individuals and gangs.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 810.040 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

157

§810.040. LODGE PUBLICATIONS.
A Lodge may publish and mail a Lodge bulletin informing the members of the
Lodge of its activities and including news items relating to any of the Masonic
Organizations so as to promote Masonic intercourse. The bulletin may be a joint
publication of the Lodge and one or more other Lodges and Masonic Organizations
if each participating organization pays its prorata share of the cost to publish and
mail the bulletin. However, the sponsors of a joint publication may permit any
Masonic Youth Order to include material in the publication without charge, and
the sponsors may assume the cost of mailing the publication to members of the
Masonic Youth Order.
The foregoing notwithstanding, no Lodge may publish in the public domain
any personally identifying information about a Mason of the Lodge without the
affirmative written consent from that Mason.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 810.050 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§810.050. LODGE ROSTERS.
A Lodge may publish a roster for Masonic purposes and for the benefit of its
Masons containing the names, mailing addresses and telephone numbers of all
of its Masons. A Lodge may also include in its published roster an electronic
mail address for a Mason of the Lodge with his permission. However, no Lodge
may publish in the public domain any personally identifying information about
a Mason of the Lodge without the affirmative written consent from that Mason.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to require a member to give
his consent before his personal information may be published to the public.
This Resolution specifies that no Lodge may publish in the public domain any
personally identifying information about a Mason of the Lodge without the
consent of that person.
Section 810.040 of the California Masonic Code specifies that bulletins
published by Lodges are to inform members of the Lodge of its activities. CMC
Section 810.050 specifies that Lodge rosters containing names, mailing addresses
and telephone numbers are for the benefit of its members. Email addresses may
be included if the member has given his permission.

158

Proceedings of the

Resolution Number 2010-12 would have expanded Lodge rosters to
include such information as spouses names, birth dates, anniversary dates, etc.
The report of this committee on that Resolution included the concern for identity
theft and privacy issues, and that Resolution failed to pass.
While the Appendix on Grand Masters’ Decisions titled “Use of Social
Networks and Websites 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No 4” states that a Lodge,
a Masonic group and a Mason may have a presence on social networking sites like
Facebook and Myspace, it does not include rosters of any kind.
Protection against identity theft and privacy should always be a concern
and it has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge to maintain the privacy of
its members.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.
