Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

251

Report of the President of the Board
Masonic Homes of California
July 2012-June 2013
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
Providing services in the name and on behalf of every Mason in
California, your Masonic Homes is committed to assisting California Freemasons
and their families throughout their lives, and particularly when they are the most
vulnerable. Throughout all the changes in our programming, and as we expand
and change to reflect the changing face of our fraternity, our commitment to this
core mission never wavers.
It has been a busy and exciting year as we have adopted a new governance
model and are going through a leadership transition as we are currently conducting
a search for a new executive vice president. This change in leadership comes at
a pivotal moment for our fraternity. Our membership demographics are shifting
and within the next few years, an increasing number of our members will be
caring for children and aging parents. Many will require assistance from the
Masonic Homes of California – some through Masonic Outreach Services and
others through our residential communities. Changes in health care have also
been taking place throughout our country, both in terms of regulations and in how
society views retirement and aging. The Masonic Homes must, of course, evolve
with these changes. We are confident that we will find a leader who reflects our
values and ensures our ability to meet these changing needs and demands.
This year we focused on defining and cultivating a high quality of life
for our residents. Our first obligation is to provide a high quality of care but that,
while an essential component, does not in itself translate into quality of life. To
learn more about how to define quality of life, we held focus groups with our
residents to arrive at a definition that was broad, inclusive, and meaningful. From
those discussions, the Board adopted the following: “Quality of life is defined as
the ability to function physically, emotionally, socially, and spiritually at a level
consistent with individual expectations and capacities.”
Having defined quality of life, we are now working on a plan for
promoting and measuring it. To do this, we turned to experts at the University of
Buffalo’s Institute for Person-Centered Care to help us develop a new approach to
care planning and outcome measurement that specifically focuses on supporting
the quality of life of our residents – however they choose to define it.
We have also focused on improving our support to our most vulnerable
residents – those impacted by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. To that end, we
are nearing completion of a renovation of Traditions, our secure memory care
unit on our Union City campus, and are finalizing plans for a new day treatment
program to be housed in the former administrator’s home. We have brought in

252

Proceedings of the

national experts to help us develop a new approach to assessment, care planning,
programming, and staff training, and are seeing significant improvements in our
resident experience as a result of these activities.
We are also focused on a plan to achieve the full value of all of our
assets, including those currently underutilized, which include:
•

Renovating the former children’s home on our Covina campus for ADA
accessibility and pursuing leases with community service organizations
for those houses.

•

Identifying and responding to opportunities and challenges posed by
health care reform, with a particular focus on developing programming
in the currently empty floor of our skilled nursing facility.

•

Exploring the possibilities for the 63 acres of frontage property on our
Union City campus.

In addition to our residential services, we offer Masonic Senior Outreach
Service (MSOS) to keep our brothers and their wives or widows in their homes
and/or home communities. MSOS provides case management to each of our
clients and financial assistance for those whose needs are greater than their means.
MSOS continues to grow each year, as many of our elderly brethren
and their wives and widows experience ongoing economic difficulties related to
living longer than planned and to their increasing care costs. We also see another
trend, in which members are seeking early retirement due to loss of employment
and/or health related issues. Both of these factors have contributed to the
growing increase in clients needing MSOS. This year, 235 members received
direct financial assistance through MSOS; another 60 received ongoing case
management services; and approximately 1,200 members received information
and referrals though our Masonic Assistance office. The generous support of
Masons who give to the Annual Fund ensures we are always in a position to the
meet the increasing and diverse needs of our most vulnerable members.
Finally, MSOS made great strides this year with the creation of its very
first Client Handbook. The Handbook is given to all new clients and explains in
detail all of the program rules and processes. Additionally, MSOS created its very
first newsletter. The MSOS newsletter will have multiple publications each year,
featuring program highlights, exciting news about our clients, and updates about
outstanding lodge partnerships. The MSOS newsletter will help foster a sense of
“extended community” for our clients, their families, and lodges.
The Masonic Assistance line, as the single point of inquiry for all
Masonic Assistance programs has made it easier for callers to obtain information
about any of our resources. The Masonic Assistance telephone number is printed
on the new dues cards, so that it is readily available.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

253

During this past year, the Masonic Assistance staff also streamlined the
application materials and made them available in electronic format. We have found
that many of our members, their families, and our lodges prefer to use electronic
forms since they can be sent via email and can be completed in a timely manner.
This single change has significantly improved the timeliness of the application
process. On average, the current application process is completed within
30-45 days.
Lodge Outreach Initiative
Masonic Outreach Services and San Diego Division IX have partnered
to develop the Lodge Outreach Initiative. This strategic initiative has focused
on strengthening partnerships with our lodges by formalizing communication
processes and developing trainings materials and tools that will be utilized
by lodge leaders as they fulfill their fraternal obligation of providing relief to
their members. During the first year, MOS and San Diego Masonic leaders
met quarterly to develop strategies to educate the membership about Masonic
Assistance programs. Together, training tools were developed to assist lodge
leaders in conducting outreach to their members in an effective manner, with the
overarching goal of ensuring our most vulnerable members and their widows do
not fall outside of the care and support of their lodges.
During this second year of the Lodge Outreach Initiative, San Diego
Division IX identified the role of training coordinators, who serve as trainers to
the lodges within their district and actively partner with MOS, serving as a liaison
to their district. The second year kicked off with an all-day training at the Masonic
Home at Covina, where training coordinators received a training binder and
actively participated in problem-solving scenarios and identifying appropriate
plans of action. This training provided training coordinators with the information
needed to access outreach services as well as how to conduct outreach. The
quarterly meetings have continued in San Diego and provide ongoing education
and support for strengthening our fraternal safety net. The training coordinators
share their stories of success and how their lodges are conducting outreach. The
success of the Lodge Outreach Initiative is reflected in the lives of the members
who have been touched by the great work of the San Diego Masonic leaders. We
have seen an increase in members referred to our Masonic Assistance program
and in those rescued from dire situations.
The Lodge Outreach Initiative will continue in Division IX and will
be extended to Division II this coming year. We will further test the success of
this initiative and extend outreach education to our lodges in the north. Through
our strategic efforts together, we believe we will redefine relief and enhance the
delivery of services and programs for our members. Through our collaborative
and innovative work together, we believe that we will be better positioned to meet
the needs and interests of our members, across the generational spectrum.

254

Proceedings of the
Child and Family Services

Masonic Center for Youth and Families
Recognizing that the shift in the demographics of our fraternity means
that more of our members are actively engaged in parenting, we are continuing
to develop our programming and approach for child and family services. The
Masonic Homes has been helping children for more than 100 years. Over the
years the Masonic Homes has been frustrated with the inconsistent results
from various methods used to diagnose children with learning, emotional, and
behavioral difficulties. The Homes joined forces with experts to come up with
a comprehensive method to combine the different disciplines that treat children
into one diagnostic regime with the hope that it will identify all of the issues
impacting the child. As a result, in 2011, the Masonic Homes opened a cuttingedge diagnostic and treatment center called the Masonic Center for Youth and
Families (MCYAF).
The outcome data generated by MCYAF is demonstrating that we are
changing the lives of children, families, and, by extension, our communities,
through the effective diagnosis and treatment of underlying issues. Researchers
and providers from around the world are paying close attention to our efforts and
to that end, Terrence Owens, Ph.D., our clinical director, recently published an
article about our unique and innovative model of care in the March 2013 issue of
“The Journal of Infant, Child, and Adolescent Psychotherapy.” Upon approving
the article for publication, the editors of the journal felt that the issues raised
and the MCYAF model of care were so important that they commissioned two
internationally renowned clinicians/authors to respond to Dr. Owen’s article.
Dr. Paul Williams (England) and Dr. James McCarthy (New York) wrote papers
expressing their strong support for the MCYAF model and the hope that such a
model will find the necessary funding and support to be widely replicated.
The editors of this journal went on to ask Dr. Owens to be a regular
reviewer of articles published in their journal; forwarded his paper to the editors
of Routledge, who offered him the prospect of a book on the MCYAF model;
and helped secure an invitation for him to present the paper at the American
Psychoanalytic Association’s annual conference in January of this year. This
presentation was so well-received that Dr. Owens was recently informed that he
has a reserved spot for presentation for the next seven years. It is a competitive
and complicated process to secure a single presentation in such a forum – the
offer of a standing presentation for seven years is rare and demonstrates the strong
interest in the outcomes and possibilities of the MCYAF model of care.
Children’s Home Alumni
At the time of the Masonic Homes Children’s Residential Program
closure in 2009, there were a total of 21 child residents. Of the 21 residents,
three had just graduated from high school and the remaining 18 stayed within

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

255

an “extension of our care” through the Children’s Transition Program. The
Masonic Homes’ commitment toward these children’s care ensured that each
child had a safe and successful transition plan. Each child and his or her family
was assigned a care manager, who worked with the family to create safe and
stable living environments that would also meet the child’s educational needs.
Through financial support and assisting families in accessing and applying for
public benefits and low-cost programs, the children continued on their path of
success that was established during their residency at the Masonic Homes.
Since that time, the children have graduated from high school and have
pursued college through the Masonic Homes Scholarship Program. In 20122013, the Transition Program served five children and their families. Of these
five children, one child graduated from high school in June 2013 and will start
college this fall. He has also earned a scholarship through the Masonic Homes
Scholarship Program. The remaining four children will continue to be served
through the Transition Program during the 2013-2014 school year. Of these
children, three will be high school seniors and one will be a high school junior.
We look forward to our watching our youngest group of residents grow up and
embark upon their last years in high school. And while they still require some
assistance and guidance, their futures remain bright!
The Masonic Homes Scholarship Program continues to offer scholarships
to alumni of the former Children’s Residential Program. Scholarships are provided
for up to five years toward undergraduate studies; up to two years toward masters
programs; and up to five years toward doctoral programs. Additionally, scholars
are able to attend schools of their choice throughout the United States. Scholarships
are based on the type of school and students’ full-time or part-time status. A
hallmark of this program’s success has been the case management support that
is provided to ensure students access school support services and successfully
navigate through college on their way to becoming independent adults. All
scholars must maintain a GPA requirement and reapply for scholarships annually.
This has led to strengthening students’ accountability for their performance and
commitment toward their education.
During the 2012-2013 school year, the scholarship program served a total
of 13 students. The program experienced its largest group of college graduates
this year. We had a total of four scholars graduate this spring, completing their
bachelor degrees from Cal State colleges, a private university, and a professional
trade school. For the upcoming 2013-2014 school year, the Scholarship Program
has approved a total of 17 students to receive scholarships. It has been fulfilling
to witness the success of our former alumni, as they pursue a higher education
to better themselves and their futures with the continued support of the Masonic
Homes.

Masonic Family Outreach Services
In October 2009, we began providing financial and non-financial case
management to members and their families under the age of 60, a program
currently known as Masonic Family Outreach Services (MFOS). This program
was developed in response to the economic downturn and the overwhelming
need for support to our younger members. MFOS provides short-term financial
assistance, for which there are eligibility requirements and time limits. The
financial support provided is intended to serve as a bridge from economic hardship
toward self-sufficiency. An identified and agreed-upon care plan about how to
reach self-sufficiency is the lynchpin to the success of this program. All financial
clients agree to partner with their care manager toward this goal and must also
apply for and access any public benefits for which they qualify.
Case management support is extended to the entire Masonic family,
with no eligibility requirements or time limits. Case management services are
broad, flexible, and able to serve families in their own communities. Our support
includes identifying resources for families struggling with today’s complex
issues, as well as assistance with applying for public benefits and other programs.
Our care managers provide support that meets the member’s individual needs.
The Masonic Assistance line (888/466-3642) provides information-referrals to all
callers in need of community resources. We are able to serve callers with a wide
range of needs and across different age groups.
This past year, 37 clients were provided with direct financial assistance
and another 35 clients received ongoing case management. On average, MFOS
served 17 clients per month with case management and 10 clients per month with
financial case management.

and extraordinary dedication, we have achieved all of the above while laying the
foundation for the future. It has been a pleasure and an honor to serve with the
distinguished members listed below:

Report of the Directors of the
Acacia Creek Retirement Community
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Acacia Creek, our continuing care Retirement Community located
adjacent to the Masonic Home at Union City, is now in its fourth year of
operation. I am pleased to report to you that we have had a significant increase
– 62 percent - in both the number of occupied units and the number of residents
since this time last year. Our innovative use of marketing initiatives to encourage
deposits and move-ins has yielded positive results. A second duplex cottage, for
which construction was delayed pending a buyer, has now been sold and the
cottage is being built, another positive indicator of the community’s progress.
Late this summer we crossed the 100 mark in apartments occupied, another
significant milestone. Based on these numbers we will be applying for our
permanent Certificate of Occupancy from the California Department of Social
Services in 2014.
Most importantly, in a recent national survey, our residents’ satisfaction
measured well above the average. Current residents’ satisfaction and happiness
is apparent to prospective buyers, and because of this our residents continue to
be our best sales people in the community and are always involved in the sales
process. Residents invite friends and lodge brothers to join them for meals, or
for an overnight stay in the guest apartments, and “host” them for dinner and
entertainment, often resulting in a new deposit.
Masterpiece Living is a national program of physical and mental
wellness which has been adopted by Acacia Creek. Measured against the national
benchmarks for residents in similar communities, our residents show a lower level
of physical problems and a higher level of nutritional and physical activity.
The absorption of non-Masons into the Acacia Creek community has
been rewarding for both Masonic and non-Masonic residents. There is great
camaraderie among them and the community has been strengthened by adding
to the mix. Two new residents have become Master Masons and more are
expected to petition for degrees in the future. Members of Acacia Creek have
become very engaged with Siminoff Daylight Lodge at Masonic Home, Union
City, as participants, officers and in the construction of the new outdoor lodge on
the property.
The Acacia Creek staff continues to share feedback about the
positive work environment through an annual employee satisfaction survey.
During the past year, our community has experienced zero percent turnover
amongst our staff.

270

Proceedings of the

When the fraternity planned the Acacia Creek community, we envisioned
that it would include all levels of health care, including independent and assisted
living, skilled nursing and memory care. To fulfill this goal, Acacia Creek has
entered into a joint effort with the Masonic Homes to explore various initiatives
such as renovation of the Traditions section of the Union City Home and conversion
of the former Administrator’s house to an adult day care center to serve a portion
of the dementia care needs for both Acacia Creek and Masonic Homes.
The Acacia Creek Board has completed the adoption of the Policy
Governance structure of board management and is pleased with the resulting
“freedom” to pursue long-term planning agendas while maintaining assurance
that the operational needs of the organization are being met in a timely and
appropriate manner.
Earlier this spring the Acacia Creek board of directors acted to stabilize
the long term debt of Acacia Creek through a restructuring of the community’s
loan. This action will result in an overall savings of over 25 million dollars and
will enable us to pay off our debt 5 years sooner than originally planned. Not only
does this give Acacia Creek greater financial strength and viability it provides
Masonic Homes with a better guarantee that Acacia Creek can succeed without
requiring any permanent financial support from Masonic Homes. The financial
and legal staff of Grand Lodge spent many hours researching and negotiating this
action on our behalf and we owe them a large measure of gratitude for their efforts.
And our sincere appreciation to our Executive Vice President, Chuck Major, who
is the heart and soul of the management team and has been responsible for the
high level of morale and accountability of the staff.
I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee,
the Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, and the Acacia
Creek Board for their expertise, their vision, and their passion. Together we
look forward to continuing the mission of bringing Acacia Creek to stability and
financial security.
Respectfully submitted,
Michael D. Neben, President
Ara Maloyan, Vice President

Report of the Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Your California Masonic Foundation focused this year on extending the
reach of California Masons beyond the lodge and deeper into our communities
to make an even more profound difference in public education. Our programs
continue to be aligned with the strategic plan of the Masons of California and
fully supported by the Grand Lodge Executive Committee. We have increased the
visibility of the fraternity in our communities and involved larger numbers of our
members through the Public Schools Advisory Councils. We continue to oversee
a wide range of programs supporting various needs within the jurisdiction.
Strategic Initiatives
Considerable progress was made this year in furthering the two strategic
initiatives the Foundation is responsible for – support to public education and
increasing lodge involvement in the community. Our six Public Schools Advisory
Councils continued their strong leadership by organizing and conducting six Public
Schools Month kickoff celebrations in April 2013, which were attended by more
than 550 Masons, community members, and teachers. As a part of these events,
the Foundation donated more than $770,000 to support California classrooms and
students. These very successful celebrations further raised community awareness
of Freemasonry and demonstrated our dedication to both public education and the
lifelong learning of our students.
Literacy
This year we completed the second term of our groundbreaking
partnership with the leader in child literacy programs - Raising A Reader. This
nationally recognized program provides children with books and the support
necessary to develop the reading and learning skills that will allow them to
succeed academically. Equally important, the program focuses on the shared
reading experience between parent and child, encouraging family engagement,
strengthening family ties, eliminating achievement gaps, and transforming
students’ learning experiences. For example, in a San Jose kindergarten classroom,
students who participated in the Raising A Reader program were able to read more
than three times the number of words than the school’s previous standard.

272

Proceedings of the

Raising A Reader has proven so successful that the program has received
a grant from the prestigious Anne E. Casey Foundation. This organization has
worked with disadvantaged children for 60 years and will be researching the
effects of Raising A Reader’s integrated literacy/parental engagement model.
In addition, the fraternity has received positive feedback from parents and
educators throughout the state, increasing public awareness of Freemasonry
as a force for good in our communities. Please refer to the proceedings of this
Annual Communication to review a chart detailing the schools where our Public
Schools Advisory Councils, in collaboration with local partners, have introduced
Raising A Reader.
Thanks to the generosity of the Masons of California, as of this Annual
Communication, Raising A Reader will now be part of 162 California classrooms.
We are well on our way to reaching more than 20,000 students by the end of
our fifth year. The Foundation expresses its gratitude to Most Worshipful Lowe
and the Grand Lodge Executive Committee for their leadership in continuing to
support Raising A Reader as the fraternity’s project for this and the next several
years, allowing continuity and greater potential of making a profound and lasting
impact on literacy in this jurisdiction.
Middle School Math
The transition from elementary school arithmetic to the abstract concepts
of mathematics embodied in algebra and geometry can be extremely challenging
for most students. Finding a meaningful and impactful way to improve the ability
to make this transition continues to be an elusive problem. Dialogue still continues
with educators on a number of fronts, but no clear, nationally recognized, program
has emerged to meet the need and expectations of the Foundation. Continued
research and evaluation will be required next year before a viable path forward
can be implemented.
Investment in Success
The Foundation is pleased to report that thanks to the diligent efforts of
our Public Schools Advisory Councils, 90 new students received Investment in
Success scholarships this year. These recipients were nominated by their school
principals and counselors, and went through a rigorous interview and evaluation
process by Public Schools Advisory Council members in each of their areas.
Most of these students live in challenging environments with many family issues
and limited possibilities for a college education. Yet these students consistently
showed the drive to succeed, a vision for their future, and the commitment to better
themselves and to give back to their communities. Please refer to the proceedings
of this Annual Communication to review a listing of this year’s Investment in
Success scholarship recipients.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

273

In addition, the first two years of our revamped program have revealed
that community college students are facing significant challenges due to massive
budget cuts, long waiting lists, fewer course offerings, and declining support
from counselors in creating study or transfer plans. To address these issues, the
Foundation has revised the Investment in Success scholarship program to include
opportunities for summer or third year courses to increase students’ chances of
graduating and potentially moving on to a four-year school. This year we have
awarded nine such summer scholarships. These summer scholarships also provide
the opportunity to experiment and participate in bringing innovative solutions as
well as best practices to California’s higher education system.
Currently, our resources can only reach a limited number of deserving
students. But, last year alone, almost $500 million of state financial aid was left
unclaimed by students. To address this situation and allow more students to access
these funds, the Foundation has partnered with GLOW and the College Access
Foundation of California to create “College Gold Rush,” a one-stop-shop for
accessing financial aid resources and information, usable by parents, students,
and school administrators. The site is currently being updated to walk parents
and students through the form completion process. This website will increase the
number of completed financial aid applications statewide, allowing more funds to
reach more students and decreasing families’ financial burden.
The Foundation has also begun forming partnerships with college
access and student support organizations throughout the state to ensure that our
scholarship students are receiving the care and support they need to succeed. You
can be proud that, with the help of the Masons of California, more students will
be given a chance for a better, more productive life.
Public Schools Advisory Councils
The councils increased their support this year to both the literacy
and Investment in Success initiatives. Each council performed admirably and
successful Public Schools Month kickoff celebrations were conducted throughout
the jurisdiction, with attendance by the Executive Committee and Foundation
trustees. The councils worked closely with their local school districts to identify
the scholarship candidates and to conduct the interview and selection process.
Personal presentations of the scholarship awards were made where possible to
further highlight students’ accomplishments while publically reinforcing the
fraternity’s commitment to public education. Council members also visited lodges
to make presentations about Raising A Reader and to seek monetary support for
the fraternity’s project. The Board of Trustees thanks the chairs and members of
all six councils for their tireless work on behalf of the Foundation.

274

Proceedings of the

Teacher of the Year
The Foundation continued its major sponsorship this year of the
California Teacher of the Year program. The annual state banquet was held in
Sacramento and the five Teacher of the Year finalists were celebrated. Your
grand master and the foundation were present and the Masons of California were
recognized for their strong support. Each of the five Teacher of the Year recipients
was also individually honored in a celebration within his or her own community,
where the Foundation presented monetary awards and gifts.
Other Programs
The Foundation continued this year to underwrite our existing leadership
development, lodge growth and Masonic education programs, including
the Secretary and Treasurer Retreats, Master and Wardens Retreats, Lodge
Management Certification Program webinars, Inspectors Development Academy,
the Institute for Masonic Studies, and the California Masonic Symposium. In
addition, our heritage sites, historic article preservation, Henry Wilson Coil
Library and Museum, and California Masonic Memorial Temple maintenance
were funded.
Board Governance
The Board of Trustees continued to function within the governance
model adopted last year across all the major boards and committees. This year the
Foundation focused on becoming comfortable with the operations and reporting
requirements of the executive vice president as chief executive officer, and moving
more into the long-term strategic planning encompassed by the Ends policies of
the Board. The Board also held its annual strategic planning retreat and focused
on future Ends policy definition.
The Board continued to function smoothly in the new governance model,
thanks to the concerted efforts of Brad Colby, director of administration and board
governance. The Board thanks him for the countless hours spent in keeping us
organized and on track.
Looking Forward to 2014
The Foundation will enter next year with its strategic initiatives
progressing well and poised to make an ever-increasing impact on public
education. We will continue to increase the number of classrooms embracing
Raising A Reader by raising the necessary funds and involving even more of our
lodge members in the activities of the Public Schools Advisory Councils. While

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

275

we continue the effort to identify a meaningful middle school math program,
we will continue to refine our Investment in Success program and the College
Gold Rush website to increase the number of students with whom we can make a
profound difference through access to higher education. And we will continue to
work toward defining a funding pipeline approach that not only meets our Raising
A Reader goals, but will substantially increase our financial resources in order to
have a significantly greater impact on society by our 50th anniversary.
Acknowledgements
The Trustees wish to thank Most Worshipful Lowe for our appointments
and the opportunity to serve this Grand Lodge. Special thanks in particular go
to Doug Ismail, executive vice president and chief philanthropy officer; Mark
Pressey, vice president; Brad Colby, director of administration and board
governance; and the Grand Lodge staff led by Very Worshipful Allan Casalou,
grand secretary, for their continued outstanding leadership, guidance, and support
to this Foundation Board of Trustees.
Special Acknowledgement
The expansion of our Public Schools Advisory Councils and the
successful Public Schools Month kickoff celebrations, as well as the revamping
of our Investment in Success program to include summer and third year options,
would not have been achieved without the outstanding efforts of Jessica Mausner,
our manager of education and community programs. Although only with us a
short time, Jessica’s teamwork, communication, and creative skills improved our
literacy and scholarship efforts profoundly. Her efforts today will yield untold
benefits to California students, communities, and the fraternity far into the future.
We wish her well in her new pursuits and know that she will be as successful
in the future as she has been with us. The Board of Trustees thanks her for
everything she has accomplished and wishes for her the blessings of our Supreme
Grand Master.
Respectfully submitted,
Arthur H. Weiss, President

Proceedings of the

Report of the Board of Trustees

of the California Masonic Memorial Temple

Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
(CMMT) respectfully submits its 58th annual report, summarizing its activity
during the 2012-2013 Masonic year. Those interested in more detailed information
are referred to the minutes of the meetings of the Board of Trustees reposed in
the archives of our Grand Lodge. Full and audited financial statements are not
included in this report, but are included in the appendices of these proceedings.
The Board of Trustees is entrusted with the preservation, maintenance,
and future viability of the landmark CMMT facility that inspires and services
our members. The CMMT owns this magnificent edifice and derives its revenue
by leasing space to the Grand Lodge of California, whose offices are on the
third floor; to the Nob Hill Masonic Center that operates the garage and the
telecommunications facility on the roof; and to other third parties, primarily Live
Nation, who lease space in the building. We also receive tax-exempt contributions
from candidates who are initiated into our California lodges.
This year the facility celebrates its 55th year located at 1111 California
Street in San Francisco. The Temple continues to gain recognition as a resource
for cultural and social events. From the time of its opening to the present day, it
has served not only as a facility for Masonic gatherings, but also as a venue for
concerts and other events enjoyed by the greater community. The auditorium is
the second largest event space in the city of San Francisco and currently hosts
up to 54 concerts and 25 cultural or comedy events per year. It has also been
five years since we restored the Emile Norman endomosaic mural – an incredible
work of art and symbol of Masonry in California.
Over the past five years we have worked with Live Nation to bring better
efficiency in the rental of our building and to enhance its future viability. This has
been a long process involving negotiations with governmental agencies as well
as community interests. In February, we finalized a long-term agreement with
community associations, allowing us to move forward with renovation plans, and
ensuring the Temple’s future as an event space. As a part of this agreement, and
in holding with our continued community outreach, CMMT, in conjunction with
Live Nation, will make ongoing contributions in support of a new Huntington
Park Preservation Fund. Live Nation will also offer reduced rental rates for ethnic
and cultural performers.

of the Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. is unique among the various Masonicentity boards in California in that it is our only for profit, income-tax-paying entity
responsible for overseeing the efficient and profitable operations of the garage
located at the top of Nob Hill. One of our most important responsibilities is to
ensure payment of a dividend to Grand Lodge at the end of each fiscal year, which
in turn helps fund the many ways the Masons of California make a profound
difference in the lives of our members and in society. This year, I am proud to
announce that the dividend will be the largest to date.
To ensure the efficient and safe management of our garage, we have
continued our ACE Parking Agreement. ACE is one of the city’s most recognized
garage operators and has managed the day-to-day operations of the facility
well. With their help, with the creation of new parking arrangements with local
businesses, and with event parking from Live Nation, we are now generating
strong event parking revenues along with steady monthly and daily parking
revenue. With the California Masonic Memorial Temple being closed due to
construction starting in January 2014, there is a solid plan in place to manage
the planned decrease in revenues while still forecasting a dividend that meets our
Ends Policy.
We continue an agreement with Zipcar to use 24 parking spaces in our
garage, an increase from last year. We also completed an agreement with Suite
America to use 15 spaces in our garage for the corporate cars of visiting corporate
executives, and also completed an agreement with Getaround to use one space for
their ride-sharing car. These agreements ensure a steady revenue stream and make
our location a growing hub for these car-sharing services for people throughout
San Francisco.
The new security firm and the improved surveillance and security system
implemented this year will help maintain the garage’s convenient and secure 24hour access for patrons, including guests at many of the nearby hotels on Nob
Hill. The automation put in place to manage the access in and out of the garage
continues to prove itself valuable in keeping labor expenses down.
We have fully implemented the policy governance model for more
effective board management and are realizing the benefits in our board
operations by introducing a policy governance approach. We are able to focus
on the right granularity of details and on the appropriate level of information
that improves the efficiency of the board while overseeing an increase in overall
operations effectiveness.

Proceedings of the
Report of the Committee
on Finance

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Code, Section 406.035 E, requires the Committee
on Finance to review all of the proposed Recommendations and Resolutions to
be considered at the Annual Communication and to report on the financial impact
these items may have on the Grand Lodge budget.
Earlier this year, the committee reviewed the Carry-Over Resolutions and
New Resolutions as provided by the Grand Secretary. On July 30, we finalized our
report on the cost impact of each item. The Grand Secretary on August 1 posted
the report, with the legislation, to the lodges. WE have also review Grand Master
Lowe’s Recommendation No. 1.
Only one resolution was found to have any financial impact on the Grand
Lodge, and in as much as our written report has been distributed, I will report on
it now and not later during the session.
Resolution No. 13-10: Creates an Award for Twenty-Five Years of
Membership: This Resolution would require the Grand Lodge to provide an
award to members who have been Master Masons for a total of 25 years or more.
Though the award is not specified, it is presumed that the award would consist
of a lapel pin and a certificate. The per-unit cost to produce and ship the pin
and certificate is approximately $5.50. Approximately 28,500 members would be
eligible for the award in the first year. The cost to produce and distribute these pins
and certificates if requests were made for all of these members is approximately
$157,000. This is the maximum impact on the Grand Lodge budget.
Each year thereafter, approximately 600 additional members would
become eligible for the award adding additional annual cost of approximately
$3,300, plus any necessary inflation.
There are a number of Resolutions that would cause changes to the
Ritual or the Monitor. It has been a practice of the Grand Lodge to make the
printed changes and produce new ciphers and monitors only after the current
inventory has been depleted. Therefore, there is no additional expense caused by
the adoption of these Resolutions.
Again, in the view of the Committee on Finance, none of the other
legislation will have a financial impact on the Grand Lodge budget.

John C. Kempf, Jr.

Respectfully submitted,
David L. Barnekoff, Chairman
John R. Gale, Vice Chairman
Levon H. Keshishian

Report of the Committee
on Investments
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent handling
of Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist primarily of the General
and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes of California, but also include
the investment portfolios of various charitable trusts, the California Masonic
Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, the Grand Lodge Retirement
plan and the Grand Lodge itself. We take this charge very seriously. In its simplest
terms, we manage the investment funds with an eye to for grow and preserve
capital. We strive to maintain increasingly diversified portfolios that are designed
to generate the necessary funds for the continuing operation of Masonic functions
as well as allow for growth for future needs. In doing so, we constantly scan the
horizon in an attempt to manage the funds to take advantage of long-term trends
as well as nearer-term opportunities. The Grand Lodge Investment Committee
utilizes the services of professional investment management firms to gain access
to the capital markets. The funds are invested in the domestic United States,
international equity markets, and a smaller allocation is invested in global fixed
income markets. In recent years, we have increased our investment allocation in
less traditional investment vehicles that are not as correlated to the traditional
stock and bond markets.
I am pleased to report that the Grand Lodge and related entities had
positive performance over the preceding fiscal year (ending June 30, 2013). Of
particular note is the fact that early indicators point to the hard work and heavy
lifting accomplished by the committee and our consultants over the last five years
are finally bearing fruit. We continue to be cautiously optimistic that this trend will
continue. We remain committed to our investment process and the responsibilities
with which we are charged.
Grand Lodge Investment Performance
For the year ended 6/30/13
The Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio advanced 12.6%
for the year ending June 30, 2013. This result outpaced the Policy Benchmark
return of 11.2%.
The U.S. equity allocation of the portfolio was up 22.3% compared
to 21.5% for the Dow Jones Total Stock Market Index. The Non-U.S. equity
portfolio was up 14.5% compared to 13.6% for the MSCI All Country World exU.S. Index. Global Equities advanced 22.5% compared to 16.6% for the MSCI
All-Country World Index. The fixed income portfolio was up 2.3%, compared to
a negative 0.7% return for the Barclays Aggregate Bond Index. Our Alternative

286

Proceedings of the

Investments were up 4.2% versus 5.9% for the Custom Alternatives Index.
Overall, the portfolios’ allocation to public equities benefitted the Grand Lodge
and Related Entities over the past year. A more detailed manager performance
review can be found in the tables following this report.
The U.S. and world economies continue to show signs of a slow, uneven
recovery nearly five years after the 2008 recession. Job creation has been relatively
anemic during this economic recovery. Simultaneously, the unemployment rate in
the U.S. has fallen to 7.4% - primarily due to a declining job participation rate.
The Federal Reserve has kept short-term interest rates near zero in an
effort to stimulate the economy. This has driven interest rates lower while bond
prices have moved higher over the last five years. It is the opinion of the Investment
Committee that this trend has likely now reversed and interest rates will continue
to rise over time. Furthermore, the Federal Reserve continues to provide support
to the economy through the outright purchase of Treasury bonds and Mortgage
Backed Securities in a program dubbed “Quantitative Easing.” Over the last five
years, there have been three such initiatives with varying results. Specifically, these
programs have had the effect of spurring capital markets higher, just to see them
decline once the program ends. Recently, The Federal Reserve has signaled that it
is considering tapering off the latest round of stimulus. All these interventions into
the capital markets are unprecedented, in magnitude and duration, in the history
of our country. Surprisingly, in spite of the magnitude of monetary stimulus,
inflation remains subdued. We suspect this is due to financial institutions, namely
banks, being reticent to lend to all but the most well capitalized businesses and
individuals. The Federal Reserve has said they have their eye on inflation ticking
above 2.5% per annum.
The Investment Committee does not attempt to take advantage of
perceived short-term anomalies in the markets by chasing the most recent top
performing asset class. Rather, it arrives at its recommended allocation to stocks
and bonds and other asset classes only after very careful due diligence and
consideration. The purpose of the funds, their spending requirements, investment
time horizon and ability to assume risk are all factored into these recommendations.
The probability and duration of potential losses are carefully weighed against
the long-term potential for appreciation of assets after withdrawals are taken
into account. The Investment Committee recommends asset allocations that will
provide the highest probability that the funds will be able to meet their respective
objectives over the long-term.
Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance
For the year ended 6/30/13
The market value of the Masonic Home’s combined general and
endowment fund portfolios as of June 30, 2013, was $775.3 million compared

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

to $710.5 million a year earlier. This, combined with the investment portfolios of
the other entities, which the Investment Committee advises, resulted in combined
assets totaling slightly more than $826.3 million compared to $773.5 a year ago.
For the twelve-month period, ending June 30, 2013, the combined funds
of Grand Lodge and the related Masonic entities were up 12.6%. This compares
to 11.2% for the custom benchmark index.
For the three-year period ending June 30, 2013, the combined Grand
Lodge and related entities returned 10.0% versus 10.6% for the benchmark.
Since inception, our funds have returned 7.8% annually versus 7.7% return of the
benchmark. All returns are net of fees. Detailed Entity performance can be found
in the tables following this report.
Summary of Recent Changes
Over the past five years, the Grand Lodge and Related Entities asset
allocation has evolved in an effort to better position the portfolio to withstand
downturns in the markets while still maintaining the overall expected return.
For example, five years ago, the asset allocation included approximately 73%
in public equities. While public equities are an essential piece of the asset
allocation, the Investment Committee of the Grand Lodge of California has
taken steps over the past five years to reduce this allocation in favor of strategies
that provide diversification to equity risk. As such, the current asset allocation
includes approximately 55% in public equities. Capital has been re-allocated to
alternative strategies that are designed to perform well when the public equity
market struggles, thereby smoothing out the inevitable “ups and downs” of the
equity markets.
Another major strategic asset allocation change implemented by
the Investment Committee in response to the changing market environment
is in the fixed income portfolio. The fixed income portfolio is managed in an
“unconstrained” manner. This means that our investment manager has the ability
to position the portfolio to potentially withstand a rising interest rate environment.
When interest rates increase, bond prices decrease. Utilizing the skills of a bond
manager with multiple tools at their disposal has the potential to minimize the
damage of a rising interest rate environment on a bond portfolio.
Grand Lodge Investment Management
For the year ended 6/30/13
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand Lodge
Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee meets quarterly
with our Investment Consultant, Hewitt EnnisKnupp and our individual portfolio
managers. We review their respective performance compared to various indices

288

Proceedings of the

representing their objective. This process provides the Investment Committee
with the necessary data to evaluate each investment manager on a timely basis,
and to observe whether they continue to achieve the objectives of their mandate.
The committee also holds monthly WebEx conference calls to discuss
any outstanding business on a timelier basis, or discuss the implementation of
tactical changes within the portfolio.
In addition, the committee makes regular calls to the managers to assess
if there have been any material changes at the respective investment company that
may affect the management of assets, or that may be a sign of bigger potential
issues that requires further review and analysis.
Finally, we have scheduled bi-annual retreats to afford us the time to
review the strategic initiatives we implemented over the prior two years, review
the macro environment and opportunities therein and chart a course for the
following two-year period.
Our Investment Consultant, EnnisKnupp was purchased by Hewitt and
Associates in July 2010. This was followed closely by the announced acquisition
of Hewitt EnnisKnupp by Aon Corporation. The Investment Committee is pleased
with these changes and feels that there has been a marked improvement in the
quality of advice and reporting, while the integrity of the independent advice has
not been diminished in any way.
Not only is the Investment Committee responsible for managing the
portfolios of our various organizations, but it also oversees the management of our
planned gift investments. The current portfolio of planned gifts includes nearly
$10 million; including $7.5 million in charitable trusts and just over $2 million
in charitable gift annuities. Despite the obvious difficulties in our economy, the
Grand Lodge Office of Philanthropy had another successful year in the solicitation
of contributions and gifts. Particular recognition goes to our Planned Giving staff:
including Director of Development, Candler Gibson; Planned Giving Officer
Dick Kellogg; and newly hired Gift Officers in Northern and Southern California,
Greg Cherry and Julie Weinberg, who raised many charitable planned gifts from
brethren and their families this year and are engaging members interested in
leaving a charitable legacy in the future. The Investment Committee is grateful
to the entire staff at the Offices of Philanthropy and Finance for their support and
hard work this past year, and look forward to another successful philanthropic
campaign in 2013-2014.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist
individual lodges in determining appropriate investment strategy. One available
vehicle to aid in this effort is the “Lodge Investment Options Program” which
is intended to assist Lodges in determining an appropriate investment strategy
and asset allocation. Whether you currently have Lodge investments or are
considering implementing such a program, we direct your Lodge trustees’ or

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

289

investment committee members’ attention to the Member Center website for
more information on this turnkey program. We are also here to help Lodges
establish a set of policies and procedures that are designed to ensure assets are
invested according to the needs of the Lodge and to safeguard against the misuse
of funds. Investment Committee members continue to make themselves available
to the Lodges for assistance with this program and other questions regarding
Lodge investments.
Summary
It is truly an honor and a privilege to serve as Chair of the Investment
Committee of the Grand lodge Committee. I am humbled by the dedication and
hard work of my fellow committee members. It has been a wonderful learning
experience and I am very grateful to have had the opportunity to lead such a fine
group of men who serve on the Grand Lodge Investment Committee. I thank you
for the opportunity and wish to express my appreciation to the Committee for the
commitment and devotion they have demonstrated for the Masonic causes. They
have always been forthright with their opinions and expertise. I am convinced
we have the finest group of dedicated investment professionals fulfilling our very
important mission.
It has also been a pleasure to work with past Grand Treasurer Glenn
Woody, and our current Grand Treasurer, Ray Schmalz. Our CFO Tom Boyer and
his staff are a true asset to our organization. I also wish to express my gratitude
to Brad Colby, Director of Administration and Board Governance, and his team
for their tireless work behind the scenes. We are very fortunate to work with such
professional people with unsurpassed integrity.
Respectfully submitted,

Proceedings of the
Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The
Committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered
at the next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee’s view, those of Grand Master Lowe’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
In the Committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on August 1st of this year is sufficient to carry out the
intent of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master Lowe’s
recommendations which he will present in his message is sufficient to carry out
his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set
forth in it.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge website
on August 1st of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Lowe’s
recommendations require no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or
the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries
over to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.

Mark K. Ameli
Jeffrey L. Bear

Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman
David M. Ferreria, Vice Chairman
Jack R. Levitt, PGM

Paul D. Rosenberger

Report of the Committee on
Trial Review
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records of
all trials held during the past Masonic year. All Committee votes were unanimous
except where otherwise noted.
In each of the following matters, the Committee finds there was
compliance with the procedural requirements of the California Masonic Code,
that the findings were supported by the evidence and that the penalties fixed
were appropriate.
1.

In Trial Number 2613 the Accused, in 2001, applied to be and was
made a Master Mason in 2001/2002. The application form he submitted
specifically asked in query 14 “Have you ever been arrested, taken
into custody, plead guilty or nolo contender to, or been convicted of,
a criminal offense (other than a minor traffic violation)?” The Accused
answered “No” and failed to note that he had been taken in to custody
by law enforcement, held for a period of time and interviewed about
allegations that he had molested his 3 and 4 year old daughters. At a
Juvenile Court dependency trial held prior to the accused applying to be
a Mason the Juvenile Court found that he had molested his daughters.
After the state court ruling was discovered a Masonic trial was held
and is conduct with regard to his daughter and his failure to disclose
that he was taken in to custody by law enforcement were deemed to
be violations of California Masonic Code provisions. The Trial Master
fixed the penalty at expulsion.

2.

In Trial Number 2616 the Accused was an attorney who also operated
a loan modification service which was so intertwined with his law
practice that they constituted the same business. He was disbarred by
the California Supreme Court for agreeing to represent a number of
clients, accepting fees from them, subsequently doing nothing for them,
failing to return unearned fees and failing to communicate with clients,
all violations of the State Bar Rules of Ethics. The California Supreme
Court Order of Disbarment was based upon the findings of fact and
recommendations resulting from the proceedings held in the State Bar
Court. The Bar Court’s proceedings included a formal stipulation signed
by the Accused. In the Stipulation, it was agreed that there were 18 client
victims. Additionally, State Bar Client Security Fund made payments
to an additional number of clients in excess of 100 who also had been
allegedly victimized.

294

Proceedings of the
Our law provides, in pertinent part, that unmasonic conduct consists of
“Any violation, before or after initiation, of any portion of the moral
law [CMC 1401.010(B)]” or “Any action or failure to act in vilation of
the requirements of this Code, the General Regulations of Masonry, the
Ritual or the laws, rules or regulations of the United States or of any other
governmental entity which involves the breaking of a promise, trust or
confidence or which involves moral turpitude.” The Accused’s conduct
clearly qualifies as unmasonic conduct under the foregoing section
since he repeatedly broke promises; the trust of his clients; breached his
fiduciary obligations and his duty of trust and confidence to numerous
clients by not handling their cases as promised, in failing to communicate
with them and in keeping their fees when he had not earned them. But we
need to be careful that this decision does not establish a precedent; we
are not in the business of disciplining every member who is disciplined
by some regulatory agency, especially when it relates to negligence or
unintentional conduct. This decision was based only on the egregious
facts in this case and the number of clients the Accused hurt. The Trial
Master, after considering evidence in mitigation and aggravation, fixed
the penalty at expulsion. (One member of the Committee recused himself
from consideration of this matter.)
3.

In Trial Number 2624 the Accused, acting as a member of the Masonic
Center Association, made decisions and took action without complying
with the applicable provisions of the California Masonic Code, including
the recording and transferring of Association funds and obtaining the
approval of the Committee on Masonic Properties for the expenditures
in excess of $25,000 for the benefit of real property. There was testimony
presented that the Accused acted individually and without the consent of
the elected hall association directors. The Trial Master affixed a penalty
of Suspension for a definite period of time, to wit one year.

4.

In Trial Numbers 2626 and 2628 the Accused were members of a Lodge
which prior to 1980 had operated a fireworks booth apparently for the
Lodge’s benefit and for the benefit of Masonic youth groups. The Most
Worshipful H. Douglas Lemons, who was Grand Master in 1980-1981,
ordered the Lodge not to conduct such a fund raising activity. Other
requests for such permission were also denied. No requests were made
to the Grand Master during the period of time alleged in the Charges
or while the Accused were Masons. The Accused in this case became
Masons and members of the Lodge in 1988 and 1989. It appears that
prior to their initiation the Lodge had put into effect a subterfuge to hide
their involvement in the operation of the fireworks booth by turning the
control over to a Job’s Daughters Bethel. During trial testimony was
offered that showed that the Lodge member and as well other adults
staffed the booth. (No one under eighteen years of age was permitted by

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

295

law to sell fireworks.) During trial the evidence showed that the fireworks
booth permits were in the name of a Masonic organization which seemed
to be either the Lodge or the Hall Association of the Lodge. This was
explained as being the name on the original permit which, had it been
changed would have resulted in the Job’s Daughters being placed at the
back of a long list of groups seeking permits.
The fireworks booth checking account bore the name of the Bethel;
however the tax ID number was that of the Masonic Hall Association.
When the number had been attached the account was ot established at
trial. The proceeds from the booth went to the Bethel were distributed by
their vote to several groups who apparently had provided adult help to
run the booth including the Lodge of which the Accused were members.
The payments, as had been the case for many years, were reported in
the Lodge minutes as an “anonymous donation.” One of the Accused
was a signor on the Bethel’s fireworks account, but he was an adult
advisor/officer to the Bethel. The other Accused had signed various
annual permit documents related to the licensing of the booth, but
was nominally an officer of the group of adults who were involved in
getting the annual licenses. The one Accused was the Lodge Secretary
and the other was the President of the Hall Association. Neither the tax
returns filed by the Lodge nor the Hall Association reflected the donation
from the Bethel and it was not shown on any annual reports to Grand
Lodge. In June of 2010 the Grand Master issued an order arresting the
Charter of the Lodge until such time as it was assured that the Lodge was
operating in accordance with Masonic Law, including these issues and
other irregularities. The Trial Master, because of what appeared to be the
intentional avoiding of the dictates of the California Masonic Code and
the involvement of a youth group in a deception, affixed the penalty at
expulsion. Your Committee on Trial Review was deeply troubled by the
conduct of the Lodge and the members thereof. The helping of youth
groups has always been a part of what we as Masons are encouraged to
do. We are also encouraged to set an example for all youth, whether in a
Masonic youth group or not.
What occurred in this case is clearly a failure of Masons to act
appropriately. The fault predates the Accused in this case becoming
Masons and appears it had become a part of the Lodge’s culture. It is not
practical or even possible to determine what Masons were involved and
to try them all. These accused brethren were actively involved but many
were also at fault. The Lodge as a whole was equally culpable and has
received just punishment by having their Charter arrested for a period
of time. The Committee therefore recommends that the Trial Master’s
penalty of expulsion of these Brothers be set aside and that instead they
be suspended for one year.

296

Proceedings of the
5.

In Trials Numbers 2639, 2640 and 2641 the Accused were in the
Preparation Room after a Brother awaiting his Third Degree was hood
winked. One of the Accused held the candidate while another struck him
on the left side. The third Accused stood by and allowed the conduct
to take place. The candidate was also pinched on his lower back. The
Trial Master fixed the penalty for the Accused in Trials 2639 and 2640
at expulsion and the penalty for the Accused in Trial 2641 at suspension.
The Committee agrees with the Trial Master’s recommendation except
that the penalty in Trial 2641 be a suspension for one year.

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Numbers 2613, 2616, 2624, 2626,
2628, 2639, 2640 and 2641 the findings and penalties affixed
are affirmed with exception of Trial Number 2641 where the
penalty modified to a suspension for one year and in Trial
Number 2626 and 2628 where the penalty be modified to a one
year suspension.”
6.

In Trial Number 2634 the Accused was arrested, charged and pled guilty
to violating the Political Reform Act. He was a city councilman who
conspired with others to hide the source of funds he contributed to the
political campaign of another candidate for political office; he did this
because he disagreed with the objectives of the candidate’s opponent.
His arrest, plea of guilty, jail sentence in the state court proceedings all
received a great deal of publicity including reference to his Masonic
affiliation. The Accused’s Lodge held a meeting at which the Accused
answered questions about the court case. The Lodge voted that they
would take no action on the matter and have, in other ways, indicated
their support of the Accused. The Accused waived his right to a Masonic
trial and pled guilty. The Trial Master imposed a penalty of a one
year suspension.
The Committee on Trial Review can appreciate that the Accused readily
admitted his guilt in both the court proceedings and the Masonic Trial
and some of the reasons supporting the penalty imposed. We believe
the tenets of Freemasonry prevent imposing such a penalty. The Charge
of the Entered Apprentice Degree states in part “As a Citizen, you are
enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of your civil duties, by never
proposing or countenancing any act which may have a tendency to
subvert the peace and good order of society; by paying due observance
to the laws under whose protection you live; and by never losing sight

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

297

of the allegiance due to your country.” We are also taught that it is our
“. . . up-right conduct [which] merits the honor [of being made a Master
Mason].” The Accused subverted the peace and good order of society
and did not pay due observance to the laws under whose protection we
live, and brought dishonor on the fraternity. The Committee on Trial
Review recommends that the penalty imposed by reversed and a new
and different penalty of expulsion be imposed.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Number 2634 the Committee’s report
be adopted and the penalty of one year suspension be modified
to expulsion.”
7.

In Trial Numbers 2617, 2618 and 2619 are related matters and charges.
They involve the failure of several brethren to properly account for
funds received and expended. In all three matters the brothers were
expelled. Due to mechanical failures there was neither an adequate
audio nor written recording of these trials. The Committee on Trial
Review could not determine if the evidence presented supported the
findings of the Trial Master and the penalty imposed. Because we cannot
properly execute our mandated task the Committee must make the
following recommendation.

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Numbers 2617, 2618 and 2619 be
reversed and that the Accused be reinstated and the cases be
consolidated for new proceedings pursuant to Chapter 14 of the
California Masonic Code.”
Three requests for restoration after expulsion have been referred to the
Committee for evaluation.
The first two Requests for Restoration involve the same incident. It
should be noted that at last year’s Annual Communication two other Brothers,
Catalino Alvarado (Trial Matter Number 05-28) and Dioscoro Puspos (Trial
Matter Number 05-30), involved in the same acts and similarly tried and penalized
requested restoration and the same was granted by this Grand Lodge. The facts

298

Proceedings of the

involving all these related cases are as follows: During the period of 2003 and
2004 a Lodge’s Senior Warden embezzled in excess of $20,000 from his Lodge;
he admitted to another brother that he had embezzled money and asked for help.
The brother notified the Master, who told the reporting brother to audit the hall
association account. An audit committee, comprised of five brothers, was formed
to audit the accounts involved. The men seeking restoration were part of that
committee. The committee did not perform the audit as directed.
The embezzling brother signed a promissory note to repay the funds
and the audit committee brethren conspired and agreed to not report the note or
the embezzlement to the Lodge because the embezzler was their friend and they
wanted him to be installed as Master.
The embezzlement finally came to light and in December, 2005, charges
of unmasonic conduct were brought against the embezzling brother and against
the audit committee members including Nelio Gonzales Alcantara (Trial Matter
Number 05-26) and Ernie Feliciano Tumalad (Trial Matter Number 05-29). A
Masonic Trial was held in May, 2006. The embezzling brother, who did not appear
at trial, was expelled. The five members of the audit committee, including the men
presenting these Requests for Restoration, were suspended at the direction of the
Trial Master. On the recommendation of this committee to the 2006 Grand Lodge,
the suspensions were upgraded to expulsion.
The incident and the expulsion occurred more than seven years ago. Two
of the six accused had applied for restoration and were given due consideration
and as such are now enjoying the benefits of membership in a Masonic Lodge.
Both Alcantara and Tumalad admitted the following:
1.

They knew the theft had occurred and who had embezzled
the funds.

2.

Neither of them notified the Lodge’s membership of the theft.

3.

They claimed to have participated in the hall association audit
when in fact they had not.

4.

They concealed the theft after the embezzler signed a promissory
note to repay the funds.

5.

They did not consider the embezzlement a crime because he
had signed the promissory note.

6.

They wanted the embezzler to be installed as Master in
November 2003 and that was why they did not confirm the theft.

On January 3, 2013, at a Stated Meeting of South West Lodge No. 283 F.&
A.M. the membership present voted upon a resolution requesting the restoration
of Mr. Alcantara to the rights and privileges of Masonry in California. The result
of the vote on that resolution was: Affirmatives 35, Negatives 1, Abstentions 0.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

299

South West Lodge submitted the following information in behalf of
Mr. Alcantara. He is an electrical engineer for the Department of the Navy in
San Diego, California since 1980. This job required an extensive Department of
Defense background investigation. Mr. Alcantara handles multi-million dollar
construction projects and has received numerous meritorious, excellence and
special acts awards. He donates to the department of defense Combined Federal
Campaign, American Lung Association, American Cancer Society and Disabled
American Veterans. He is active in his hometown association to aid the quality
of life and helped raise funds for restoration of a local church. He donates to
Masonic casues and volunteers at his local church activities.
He has communicated both orally and in writing with his former Lodge.
In those reciprocations he acknowledged that although his actions were done with
brotherly love the method he chose to use violated the Masonic Code he had
sworn to uphold.
On March 2, 2013, at a Stated Meeting of South West Lodge No. 283 F.&
A.M. the membership present voted upon a resolution requesting the Restoration
of Mr. Tumalad to the rights and privileges of Masonry. The results of the vote on
the resolution were: Affirmatives 40, Negatives 2, Abstentions 2.
Mr. Tumalad served in the U.S. Navy and honorably retired after 24
years of military service. He had four overseas deployments during his career.
He is a member and is current president of Rotary Club District 3790 in Orio
Bataan, Philipines in May 2013. The club supplies all public grade schools with
computer labs. He also spearheaded a Walk-A-Thon, Christmas caroling and
fund raiser events for town projects; river debris clean up, coastal trash clean
up, hazardous objects clean up assoiated with waterborne disease plaguing the
population, the planting of trees to improve the environment and disaster relief
for typhoon victims.
In regard to the offense, Mr. Tumalad indicated he will be more
circumspect in his actions, seek proper consultations, avail himself of the CMC as
his guide and avoid hastily made decisions. As noted above over seven years have
passed since the trial in this matter.
Based on all of the foregoing information and while still recognizing
the seriousness of the offenses which caused the expulsions in the first place,
the Committee is now of the opinion that the time has come. These two former
brothers have amply demonstrated that they are truly sorry for their offenses and
have repeatedly demonstrated that they are capable of being good and faithful
Masons and, most importantly, the Committee is of the opinion that the likelihood
of their recidivism is very low.
The guidelines for restoration were enacted when, in 2009, this Grand
Lodge approved Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3 (2009 G.M. Decision
No. 3). These brothers have demonstrated that they fall within those guidelines.
